9 Bodily Changes That Happen a Month After Taking Testosterone

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1588 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Menshealth

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved.
  • TESTOSTERONE GOES BEYOND building muscle.
  • Testosterone replacement therapy (TRT) can help raise T levels.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

TESTOSTERONE GOES BEYOND building muscle. T helps you maintain muscle mass, facial and body hair, sex drive, and red blood cell production. So when your T levels start to decline—which happens naturally in your thirties—there’s a whole range of symptoms like low libido or just feeling blue.

Testosterone replacement therapy (TRT) can help raise T levels. After a couple of weeks to a month, you’ll start to see some changes, some big and small. Some pleasant and not so pleasant. Below, urologists explain what happens to your body a month after taking testosterone.

Sources indicate that IF YOU HAVE low T, your doctor will conduct some tests to see if you’re a good candidate for the therapy. Ryan Smith, MD, urologist specializing in men’s health at the University of Virginia Health, claims a doctor will perform two blood tests in the morning (on different days) when testosterone is at its highest.

Low is considered under 300 nanograms per deciliter (ng/dL) by some accounts and under 264 ng/dL by others. Doctors also factor in any symptoms you’re having, like trouble getting erections or orgasms, fatigue, or just feeling blah.

Nowadays, testosterone is more accessible without a prescription, with many people only having to complete an online assessment. Leaving out a doctor’s approval and supervision, however, can be harmful, states Justin Dubin, MD, urologist at Baptist Health.

In a 2022 study that Dr. Dubin co-authored, researchers found that many online platforms are not providing testosterone therapy in accordance with the American Urological Association and the Endocrine Society guidelines. Using a secret shopper, the researchers found that the platforms offered therapy to men who didn’t meet the guidelines and didn’t mention the risks or benefits of testosterone therapy.

Working with a doctor ensures that you’re prescribed testosterone only when you need it and that you’re taking the right dose. Then, they can work with you to make sure your testosterone levels respond appropriately. Doctors like to recheck everything every six months to make sure you’re not having any negative side effects.

A number of testosterone options are available. You can choose between injectables, topical gels, creams, under-the-skin pellet therapy, pills, and nasal sprays. You can learn more about them here.

It has been revealed that each comes with its own set of side effects, so it all comes down to your personal preference, health situation, and what your insurance covers. You can read about the real-life experiences of guys of different ages and body types and their experiences with taking testosterone.

In a recent development, IT CAN TAKE a few weeks to a month or two to see your symptoms improve after starting testosterone replacement therapy, says Dr. Smith. Here are some of the side effects—some obvious and some not—that come with testosterone therapy.

It has been revealed that when you’re low on testosterone, you might notice your sex drive dip. But when you take TRT, the treatment reactivates the androgen receptors in the part of your brain that controls desire, notes Abraham Morgentaler, MD, associate clinical professor of urology at Harvard Medical School and author of Testosterone for Life. Regaining a healthy sex drive is one of the biggest benefits of testosterone replacement therapy, he says.

In a recent development, TRT may also make your erections more satisfying, though this isn’t the only piece of the puzzle. Erections also rely on healthy nerves and blood flow. That means that testosterone therapy by itself won't always help erectile dysfunction.

Muscles respond to testosterone and starting TRT can increase muscle mass, notes Dr. Morgentaler. That’s because testosterone activates the androgen receptors in muscle tissue to stimulate growth.

The effect of a testosterone replacement dose on your muscles, however, is fairly minimal. To make the most of this muscle-building benefit, you’ll need to be doing your part through strength training and possibly raising the amount of protein you consume (depending on your current intake). Don’t know where to start? Check out MH’s four-week muscle building guide.

Some men also report fat loss. While testosterone doesn’t directly incite fat loss itself, part of it may be thanks to the uptick in muscle mass. The more muscle you have, the higher your basal metabolic rate (BMR). That means your body will burn more calories at rest.

Another indirect way testosterone can help with fat loss is motivation to keep pushing once you see results. Jed Kaminetsky, MD, urologist at NYU Langone Medical Center, testosterone can increase your energy levels, making it easier to get up and sweat it out.

Sources indicate that fatigue is a common symptom of low T. “When we treat them, a lot of men will say that their energy has improved,” indicates Dr. Morgentaler.

Scientists studying testosterone aren't sure exactly how the hormone plays a role in energy—just that it does. One of the prevailing hypotheses Dr. Morgentaler can get behind is that testosterone somehow affects your mitochondria (that organelle you learned in high school is the powerhouse of your cells). The theory is that “testosterone turns them on, so they're more productive in terms of creating the energy that the cells need.”.

Sources indicate that ronald Tamler, MD, PhD, associate professor of medicine at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, says changes in energy may also be tied back to androgen receptors. “If they don't get sufficient input, that can cause fatigue,” he says. Bringing testosterone levels back up can help reverse this.

Experts don't have a definitive answer to why testosterone impacts mood so deeply—after all, “the brain is a complicated thing,” claims Dr. Tamler. But the positive effect of TRT on mood is a potential life-changing benefit.

It has been revealed that an old but highly referenced clinical trial in 2003 looked at how testosterone gels affected middle-aged men with treatment-resistant depression and low T. After 8 weeks, the men indicated greater improvements in the psychological aspects of depression (sadness, guilt, and anxiety) than those given a placebo. The men taking testosterone gels also showed nearly the same rate of improvement in somatic aspects of depression (improvements in sleep, appetite, and libido). A more recent review of 27 clinical trials involving 1,890 men with low T found that TRT provided a significant reduction in depressive symptoms, especially at higher doses.

One of the most notable things to know before starting TRT is that the treatment decreases sperm production and may cause infertility.

According to recent reports, testosterone might affect the size of your testicles, too. "Most of the size of the testicle is dedicated to making sperm, so when you're making less sperm, the testicles get smaller," says Dr. Morgentaler.

Sperm production may or may not go back to normal even after stopping treatment, states Dr. Kaminetsky. One study found increasing age and longer TRT linked to lower chances of normal sperm recovery.

It has been revealed that some people notice a little swelling in their feet and ankles because testosterone can encourage your body to hold onto excess fluid, says Dr. Morgentaler.

This isn't a big deal for most people, he notes, and swelling is more common if you're taking a non-daily treatment like an injection, when you're getting a higher dose of T in one sitting.

Testosterone replacement therapy may change your skin type—for better or for worse, says Dr. Morgentaler.

Testosterone can increase oil production, which isn't necessarily a bad thing. Oil production is crucial for healthy skin, so you may actually end up with a better complexion. However, too much oily buildup can lead to breakouts.

While Dr. Morgentaler notes testosterone-induced breakouts aren’t common, they are more likely to occur in men with a history of acne. Skin changes may also be more common if you’re taking testosterone injections versus other modes of administration since you're getting a higher dose all at once.

According to recent reports, in all men—whether you’re taking T or not—some testosterone is converted into the hormone estradiol, a form of estrogen. In men who naturally have more breast tissue, testosterone can be converted into estradiol, which may stimulate breast tissue to grow.

This is called gynecomastia, states Dr. Morgentaler, and it's not as common as other side effects. If gynecomastia does happen, your doctor will likely stop treatment for a month or two to allow your breast tissue to go back to normal. Then, you’ll resume T along with a drug that blocks the conversion of testosterone to estradiol.

If you’re going the topical testosterone therapy route, one issue to watch out for is transference with women and children.

Darshan Patel, MD, assistant professor of urology at the University of California San Diego’s Men’s Health Center, indicates testosterone from gels or creams can be transferred through skin-to-skin contact or from clothing and absorbed by someone else.

“You really have to be careful to wash your hands well and not expose others,” adds Dr. Smith. Contact with excess testosterone can affect children’s genitalia and cause premature pubic hair development and aggressive behavior.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Toyota is recalling 19,000 electric C-HR SUVs globally, with about 10,000 affected in the US.

In September, Toyota issued a safety recall involving certain model-year 2026 C-HR electric SUVs in North America.

Toyota initially remarked about 10,000 models were involved, but later confirmed the number was 8,521 in a letter to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA).

In a recent development, according to Germany’s federal motor authority, Kraftfahrt-Bundesamt (KBA), the recall has now expanded to 19,000 C-HR vehicles globally. In Germany, the recall impacts 1,096 vehicles and is still under investigation by the KBA.

Recent findings suggest that the matter stems from faulty software programming in the EV-ECU. While it’s intended to limit the battery’s charge level, the software can cause it to overcharge under certain conditions.

Toyota said the issue occurs if the battery is already at a high state of charge and the driver continues using the regenerative braking system.

When this happens, warning lights and a sound will alert the driver, and the electric drive system can shut down, causing the vehicle to lose power while driving.

Following an internal investigation, Toyota noted in the NHTSA report that the issue was caused by incorrect software that disrupted the charging-limit function, allowing the battery to overcharge while driving.

The Toyota C-HR vehicles included in the recall were produced between June 17, 2025, and July 9, 2026.

In Europe and other overseas markets, Toyota sells the C-HR EV as the C-HR+ to distinguish it from the gas- or hybrid-powered version.

OTA would be great, but there are some systems that are isolated and can't be updated that way. The EV-ECU is a core function system that is very likely sealed to prevent tampering. They never expected to need to reprogram it. It's like the firmware on your phone.

Owners of affected vehicles in North America can take them to a Toyota dealership, where the battery ECU software will be updated free of charge.

According to recent reports, toyota mailed owner notification letters out on October 18, 2026. Owners can contact Toyota’s customer service at 1-800-331-4331. The recall number is 26TA17.

Industry observers note that other than saying the EV-ECU is being reprogrammed, Toyota has not yet announced next steps for owners of affected vehicles outside North America. The KBA reference number is 17116R.

Check back for more details. The recall only affects the 2026 C-HR. The 2027 Toyota C-HR is also now on sale.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Mammograms are widely used to help detect breast cancer, but they may also offer insight into heart health.
  • The routine X-ray screening may identify breast arterial calcification (BAC), which is the presence of calcium deposits within the walls of the small arteries in the breast.
  • On a mammogram, BAC is commonly identified as thin, white, parallel lines that give a “tram-track” appearance.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mammograms are widely used to help detect breast cancer, but they may also offer insight into heart health.

The routine X-ray screening may identify breast arterial calcification (BAC), which is the presence of calcium deposits within the walls of the small arteries in the breast.

On a mammogram, BAC is commonly identified as thin, white, parallel lines that give a “tram-track” appearance.

While BAC is harmless to the breasts, it is associated with a significantly higher risk of cardiovascular disease. A 2022 study found women with BAC were 51% more likely to develop heart disease or experience a stroke than those without it.

Laxmi Mehta, MD, a cardiologist at The Ohio State University Wexner Medical Center, mentioned BAC is associated with cardiovascular risk factors, such as diabetes, high blood pressure, and high cholesterol. Additionally, BAC has been connected to:.

“The reasons for BAC resulting in higher risks for cardiovascular disease are not definitely determined; however, there are some potential mechanisms, one being that they share similar risk factors that result in vascular injury or metabolic stress that result in vascular calcification and atherosclerosis,” Mehta told Healthline.

Cheng-Han Chen, MD, interventional cardiologist and medical director of the Structural Heart Program at MemorialCare Saddleback Medical Center, added that because BAC and heart disease share many of the same risk factors, “calcium in breast arteries therefore suggests disease in the heart (coronary) and brain arteries as well,” he told Healthline.

While 1 in 39 females in the United States dies from breast cancer each year, cardiovascular disease causes one out of every three deaths, resulting in 1 death per minute.

“Cardiovascular disease is still the most common cause of death in premenopausal women,” Richard Reitherman, MD, PhD, a radiologist and medical director of breast imaging at MemorialCare Breast Center at Orange Coast Medical Center, told Healthline.

“The presentation of cardiovascular disease in premenopausal women is notoriously different than in postmenopausal women, primarily [because] there are no typical symptoms such as chest pain.”.

Reitherman stated that a prevalent and common health screening procedure such as a mammogram can lead to the early identification of women with silent cardiovascular disease.

“Cardiovascular outcome studies that have included breast arterial calcifications as a risk factor are increasingly reported in the medical literature,” he said.

“The hope is that identifying younger women with silent cardiovascular risks [like BAC along with] appropriate integrated risk identification, analysis, and interventions can significantly reduce mortality in this age group.”.

Mehta said there are several reasons BAC has been overlooked as a risk factor for heart disease.

“Mammograms are completed for assessment of breast cancer, and BAC has been historically an ‘incidental’ finding, which is not clinically relevant from an oncologic standpoint,” she said.

Additionally, there is no standardization on quantification of BAC severity, nor is it a required component of mammogram reports, said Mehta.

However, routine reporting of BAC on mammograms is an urgent goal of the American College of Radiology, Society of Breast Imaging, and Medicare, stated Reitherman.

In fact, it is gaining traction in the United States. A newly introduced Maryland law, passed on October 1, requires mammography centers to notify women when a BAC is detected on their mammogram.

“Automated identification and reporting of these calcifications detected on screening mammograms will become increasingly prevalent in the coming months [and] years,” said Reitherman.

The next step is to identify this group of women to primary care physicians so that appropriate risk evaluation can take place, Reitherman added.

In addition to doctors routinely screening for conditions related to heart disease, such as diabetes, high blood pressure, and high cholesterol, he hopes BAC will also be routinely considered.

“Under current development are protocols to identify patients needing a cardiologist’s training and expertise to appropriately stratify this group of patients,” noted Reitherman.

“The common healthcare behavior [of] having regular mammograms not only reduces risk of morbidity and mortality from breast cancer but will hopefully contribute to the reduction of morbidity and mortality from cardiovascular disease in younger women.”.

He noted this type of integrated healthcare approach demonstrates cross-specialty integration and coordination among women, radiologists, and their healthcare providers to improve women’s lives.

“This is an amazing game-changing opportunity,” Reitherman mentioned.

Mehta said it’s reasonable for women to ask if BAC is present on their mammogram report.

“But if it is not uniformly reported by the radiologist, the individual clinician may not have the answer,” she remarked.

More research is needed before BAC on mammograms can be used routinely to predict heart disease.

Finding out your BAC could provide additional information to help you and your doctors decide how aggressively to address your cardiovascular risk factors, Chen remarked.

Reitherman agreed. “The goal of reducing morbidity and mortality from any cause such as cardiovascular disease is based on recognition of risk factors, followed by appropriate lifestyle and pharmacologic interventions,” he remarked.

Latest Update: When Casual Dating Comes With Major Expectations

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (853 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Updated November 23, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk.
  • Industry observers note that A “situationship” is more than a casual hookup, but it’s not exactly a committed relationship, either.
  • Industry observers note that situationships appear to be on the rise, but what do we actually know about them from a scientific standpoint?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Updated November 23, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk.

Industry observers note that A “situationship” is more than a casual hookup, but it’s not exactly a committed relationship, either. While there may be sex, emotional intimacy, and even regular dates, it stops short of an established relationship because the partners involved don’t have a clear or mutually agreed understanding of where things stand.

Industry observers note that situationships appear to be on the rise, but what do we actually know about them from a scientific standpoint? For example, do men and women tend to approach them differently? And do they ever turn into romantic relationships?

New preliminary research offers intriguing insight into the nature of situationships.

In this study, researchers surveyed 390 adults, most of whom were from the United States, United Kingdom, or Canada. Participants ranged in age from 18 to 75 and were asked to report on relationship experiences that “exist between casual dating and committed partnerships” that “typically lack clear labels or commitment.”.

It has been revealed that they were asked about their history with situationships, including how many they’d had, as well as their motivations for pursuing such arrangements and their expectations around sexual exclusivity. They were also asked to define what a situationship means in their own words.

Qualitative analyses indicated that the most common features of a situationship included the following:.

What these findings tell us is that most people seem to understand situationships as sexual and intimate connections that feature a lot of relationship-like behaviors, but exist in a very ambiguous and unclear state.

According to recent reports, the results also indicated that men and women differed in terms of how they approached situationships. For example, women were significantly more likely than men to report entering these relationships with the hope that they would eventually develop into a committed partnership. They were also more likely to see long-term romantic potential.

Industry observers note that however, women were especially likely to describe situationships as emotionally confusing or characterized by mixed signals. In fact, 77 percent of women compared to 50 percent of men noted that situationships involve moments of closeness followed by distance. Likewise, 65 percent of women (vs. 44 percent of men) described situationships as carrying on without really progressing toward anything.

These findings suggest that, on average, men tend to approach situationships more casually, whereas women are more likely to view them as a possible stepping stone to a full-fledged romance.

Recent findings suggest that it’s important to reiterate that these are average (not universal) sex differences. However, whenever people enter a relationship with different expectations, there’s extra potential for disappointment.

One of the most striking findings was just how rarely situationships actually turned into romances.

Overall, 56 percent of participants said they had entered a situationship hoping it would later become a relationship. However, just 9 percent of past situationships eventually made the transition.

In other words, if you’re hoping for more from a situationship, odds are that it probably won’t work out, despite the fact that these relationships aren’t necessarily brief and are often recurring. In fact, about 41 percent of past situationships lasted at least seven months, with about one-quarter lasting for a year or longer. Also, half of participants reported that they had returned to a previous situationship at some point.

In short, situationships are often prolonged, recurring connections, even when they aren't progressing toward commitment.

Recent findings suggest that despite the lack of clear labels and expectations, 55 percent of participants assumed their situationship was sexually exclusive. Moreover, 68 percent of women and 58 percent of men agreed that they would feel betrayed if their situationship partner was seeing other people.

This suggests that just because a relationship is undefined, it doesn’t necessarily mean that people enter it free of expectations. Although some might assume that regular sex, emotional intimacy, and going on dates imply exclusivity or growing commitment, their partners may be interpreting the same behaviors very differently.

As with any study, this one has its limitations. In particular, because it involved an online convenience sample, it’s not clear how representative the findings are of the broader population. Also, all participants reported on different-sex situationships, so we can’t say whether the findings would apply to people in same-sex contexts.

Sources indicate that that remarked, the findings still tell us something crucial, which is that situationships aren't necessarily problematic because they lack traditional relationship labels. The core tension is that partners often don’t understand or agree upon what their connection really means.

According to recent reports, while freedom from labels and expectations is part of the appeal of a situationship, it seems that many are still bringing certain assumptions into them. Further, escalating intimacy doesn’t necessarily signal that each partner sees a progression toward commitment.

It has been revealed that costello, S. M., Costello, W., Thomas, A. G., & Graff, M. What Are Situationships? Characteristics of an Ambiguous Relationship Type. OSF. 2026. DOI:10.31234/osf.io/t72gn_v1.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The US has installed more than 200 gigawatt-hours (GWh) of battery storage, with nearly 50 GWh coming online in the first nine months of 2026 alone.

It has been revealed that the US added 48.3 GWh of battery storage through September, up 20% from the same stretch last year, according to the latest report from the Solar Energy Industries Association (SEIA) and Benchmark Mineral Intelligence. Q3 was a little slower: The US installed 14.3 GWh in those three months, down 1% year over year.

Texas added 12.3 GWh of grid-scale batteries through September, more than any other state. Arizona came in second at 7.7 GWh, followed by California at 6.8 GWh. And 11 states had already broken their annual storage installation records with three months to go – Colorado, Massachusetts, Utah, Michigan, Georgia, Mississippi, Virginia, Iowa, Montana, Alabama, and Illinois.

According to recent reports, utility-scale batteries did most of the work in Q3, accounting for 12.2 GWh of fresh capacity. Businesses and industrial sites added another 1.3 GWh, and residential added 746 megawatt-hours (MWh). That was the best Q3 yet for home batteries, though installs through September were still down 12% year over year. Some homeowners moved up their installations last year before the federal residential clean energy tax credit ended.

Sources indicate that “States are moving from targets to centralized procurements,” noted Pete Tillotson, a senior analyst at Benchmark. In September, Newly introduced York awarded contracts for eight battery projects that can deliver about 950 megawatts (MW) combined. SEIA and Benchmark now expect 708 GWh of storage across the grid, homes, and businesses by 2030, up 3.7% from their previous forecast.

The US can also make more battery cells here. A Tennessee factory opened in July and an Indiana factory opened in October, bringing US cell manufacturing capacity to 92.4 GWh, up 50%.

Sources indicate that solar and batteries helped bring down average summer wholesale power prices by 42% in Texas’s ERCOT market and 51% in California’s CAISO market between 2021 and 2026, according to SEIA’s inflation-adjusted analysis. When batteries had power to spare during peak hours, grid operators could call on expensive power plants less often.

In a recent development, you wouldn’t know it from looking at the total on residential electric bills. The cost of generating power for households fell in both markets, but the cost of delivering it to homes rose. Overall, residential bills rose 22% at the two California utilities SEIA examined and 3% across its Texas utility sample, driven by higher transmission and distribution costs. California is upgrading its grid to reduce the risk of wildfires. Texas is expanding its grid for rising demand and make it more resilient to storms.

Recent findings suggest that the article is good with the reporting about grid tied storage, but seems to miss the forest for the trees with it comes to pricing. Texas isn't installing more grid tied storage because of altruistic intent.

It has been revealed that the storage is being added because they electricity suppliers can use it to make money. They can make money because we have a reasonably well thought out wholesale electrical market AND because that market has purchases large amounts of solar and wind generation.

That combination means that I still pay just $0.01 more per kwh than I did when I moved to this state 20 years ago. I pay 12 cents per kwh and Texas average is between 12 and 15. A functional market is what makes that work.

Industry observers note that more than 300 solar and battery storage companies in the US wrote to Congress last week asking it to pass the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act. SEIA CEO Tim Pawlenty claims the permitting bill would help get projects built faster and ease pressure on power prices. However, many Democrats feel this bill falls short. The Senate voted 70–27 on Monday to end debate on the amendment containing the bill’s text, moving it closer to a final vote.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Becky the basset hound is giving latest meaning to the term “man’s best friend.” On November 12, she walked to the Whiteface Lodge, a ski resort in Lake Placid, New York. The hotel staff immediately recognized the dog, but not because of her sparkling personality or floppy ears. Becky’s owner has dementia, and the unnamed man has disappeared before.

In a recent development, the team at Whiteface called the New York State Police (NYSP), who contacted the Department of Conservation (DEC) Forest Rangers for assistance with the search. Four NYSP officers and 14 Rangers used drones and another dog (a bloodhound) to search for the missing person. According to Charlie Foutch, the lead Ranger on the search, it was about 25 to 30 degrees Fahrenheit overnight.

At 10 a.m. the next morning, a hunter who was searching just ahead of the group heard someone fall and scream. He found the missing man off to the side of a trail in a draining area with open woods. Ranger Sabo arrived on the scene shortly after. The 69-year-old man was not wearing gloves or shoes, and was suffering from some frostbite on his feet and hands. He was still alert and talking.

“We’re always looking for live people. That’s our goal is to find a live person,” mentioned Fouch. “And a lot of people are really tough. This gentleman didn’t have shoes on when we found him in the morning or mittens or gloves, so he had been out there for some period of time at night. And he still did okay. Sometimes if you keep moving in that situation, you generate enough heat to do okay.”.

Due to his injuries and the location off the trail, a hoist was the safest and quickest way to get him to safety. Ranger Martin used a cable to hoist him up to a helicopter, while NYSP Pilot Engle flew them to the hospital.

In addition to this coordination between hunters, the NYSP, and DEC, Fouch said that Becky the basset hound made this happy ending possible.

According to recent reports, “I think if the dog had not shown up at Whiteface, that gentleman definitely would have had a different outcome,” stated Fouch. “It definitely would have been much harder to find him. He may not have survived the rest of the day and probably not another night. The dog definitely contributed to him being saved so rapidly.”.

I’ve Weighed the Same for 7 Years. My Body Has Changed Completely.

  • A FEW MONTHS ago, my friend Jack Espy stopped by Men’s Health HQ, and as we were talking shop and swapping stories with MH senior editor Ryan Brower about our favorite fitness-workout-wellness gear, I asked them both to name their single favorite product.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

A FEW MONTHS ago, my friend Jack Espy stopped by Men’s Health HQ, and as we were talking shop and swapping stories with MH senior editor Ryan Brower about our favorite fitness-workout-wellness gear, I asked them both to name their single favorite product.

Jack chose his Garmin watch and raved about its amazing battery life. Ryan named his Adidas Adizero Evo SL running shoes. As for me? It was hard: the one thing, among allll the things, that actually moves the needle? After thinking for a full 20 seconds, it finally hit me:.

Weird and kind of random, right?

I thought so, too. I’ve never cared that much about how much I weigh, mostly because I didn’t have to and I didn’t want to. I’ve always been on the leaner side, so for most of my adult life, the extent of what I knew about my weight came down to whether my pants fit.

Then, about a decade ago, I started getting more serious about putting on muscle, and my trainer at the time, the big-armed and bigger-brained David Otey, introduced me to a kind of body-composition testing, a.k.a. “bioelectrical impedance analysis,” or BIA. The tech has been used to estimate body composition for decades, and you’ve probably seen one of the more sophisticated machines at your gym or doctor’s office. Step onto a platform, grab a pair of handles, wait 30 seconds, and the machine spits out a breakdown of how much of you is body fat, skeletal muscle mass, and more.

David walked me through how BIA works: The machine sends a teeny-tiny electrical current through your body. Electricity moves more easily through lean tissue than through fat, so by measuring how that current travels through you, the machine can estimate how much fat and muscle you’re carrying.

Industry observers note that in 2019, I bought an InBody Dial H20N for my bathroom. By then, BIA was well established in the consumer “smart scale” market, and InBody’s scale was among the more advanced at-home options, using sensors at both your hands and feet to take a more complete reading of your body than the foot-only models that were common at the time. The app tracks every measurement, so I can see not just what my body looks like on any given day but how it has changed over time.

To understand why I love the damn thing, it’s vital to know that I weigh roughly the same today as when I first brought the scale home seven years ago.

A conventional (dumb) scale would look at seven years of strength training, workouts I wanted to skip, workouts I probably should have skipped, and a totally unreasonable amount of thought about what I put into my body and deliver its verdict: Congrats, you weigh the same!

It has been revealed that but the InBody tells a different story. When I look back at my results from 2019, it estimated that I carried about 84 pounds of skeletal muscle mass and 33 pounds of body fat. Today, it shows I’ve got around 95 pounds of skeletal muscle and 24 pounds of body fat. Yep: According to the scale, I’ve added 11 pounds of muscle while losing about 9 pounds of fat—all while my total body weight has barely moved. (I won’t mention that I did all this during a stage of life when building muscle, and simply holding on to it, gets harder than it was when I was 25. But I will mention Men’s Health has done an amazing guide to body recomposition that is worth checking out.).

Now, a necessary reality check: Those body-comp numbers aren’t exact measurements in the same way that the number staring back at me from a dumb scale is a measurement. They’re estimates. My hydration levels can throw them off. What I just ate can throw them off. A hard workout can really throw them off.

Industry observers note that still, in studies comparing the InBody to much fancier ways of measuring body composition, the scale holds up surprisingly well for something that lives in your bathroom. There’s even a fresh model, the H40, that Inbody says is even more precise. (I keep meaning to buy it, but then something breaks in my house and a new scale gets knocked down the priority list.).

None of this means that I obsess over whether I have 94.7 pounds of muscle on Tuesday and 93.9 on Thursday. What makes this useful to me aren’t the exact numbers; it’s the direction they’re headed in. I still don’t really care how much I weigh—I wear the same pants size as when I was 25 and 35, and all my blood work is fine. But I’m trying to carry more muscle, less fat, and a stronger, more capable body into the second half of my life. I just want to know that some of my ass-busting efforts are paying off.

A dumb scale can’t tell me that. But a smart scale—this smart scale—is giving me all the direction I need.

FIND THE INBODY DIAL H20 ON AMAZON.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Polo GTI Clubsport Concept is an all-electric, track-ready, front-wheel drive hot hatch.
  • Polo GTI Clubsport Concept can hit a top speed of 149 mph, and it can accelerate from 0-60 mph in 4.7 seconds—quicker than a Golf GTI but not quite as quick as a gas-powered Golf R—with the launch control engaged.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Volkswagen’s EV push in America has skewed practical, for the most part. The ID.4 was a generic crossover, so close to an electric take on the Tiguan that VW is actually rebranding it as the ID. Tiguan. And the ID. Buzz, whimsical styling aside, is an electric van—a very expensive electric van. But VW has not abandoned its small, fun hatchback roots in Europe, and the German brand is continuing the celebration of the 50th anniversary of its GTI sub-brand with an EV: the ID. Polo GTI Clubsport Concept, which it will debut at the Essen Motorshow later this month.

The ID. Polo GTI Clubsport Concept is an all-electric, track-ready, front-wheel drive hot hatch. VW shoehorned an electric drive system intended for larger RWD vehicles into the sub-compact ID. Polo GTI; that gives the concept outputs of 362 horsepower (up to 389 hp in short bursts) and 406 pound-feet of torque, a massive increase from the 223 hp and 214 lb-ft in the standard model.

The ID. Polo GTI Clubsport Concept can hit a top speed of 149 mph, and it can accelerate from 0-60 mph in 4.7 seconds—quicker than a Golf GTI but not quite as quick as a gas-powered Golf R—with the launch control engaged.

It has been revealed that this VW’s body is heavily modified from the standard model, as well. It features a two-door layout instead of four, flared fenders, and an enormous front splitter, diffuser, and rear wing. VW also stripped out the interior for track work by deleting the rear seat and cargo area. The two front seats are Recaro racing bucket seats with five-point harnesses, and the interior also has an integrated Tornado Red roll bar.

Sadly, this is just a concept for now. Volkswagen has not committed to building an ID. Polo GTI Clubsport, and even if the brand did, it would be unlikely to be offered in the American market. VW did reveal a very cool ID. GTI concept back in 2023, which it has claimed will be more fun than the combustion-powered GTIs. And Volkswagen, pointedly, has not ruled out bringing that car to America—though getting the pricing and timing right in the U.S., with an unstable tariff situation and variable EV incentive climate, may prove tricky.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Recent findings suggest that but no one else would.
  • In 1971, Congress cut off funding for the SST, and two years later the FAA banned civilian supersonic flight over U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that in the spring of 1967, William Shurcliff began moonlighting on a project that seemed hopeless: urging the U.S. government to stop supersonic jets. By day, the Harvard-trained physicist ran experiments at the Cambridge Electron Accelerator. By night, he spent hours writing letters—to congressmen, federal aviation officials, mayors, and newspaper editors. It was not a job he wanted. “I was hoping and praying someone else would do it,” he told The Harvard Crimson.

Recent findings suggest that but no one else would. So Shurcliff rolled out the Citizens League Against the Sonic Boom and took aim at the most expensive project in U.S. commercial aviation history at the time, the Supersonic Transport (SST) program. His opposition to the SST stemmed from research by Swedish scientist Bo Lundberg, who had written extensively on the perils of supersonic aviation, chiefly the sonic boom, which could impact hundreds of millions of people every day. Shurcliff’s goal was uncompromising. “Just as the only way to get rid of the smell of the skunk is to eliminate the skunk,” he told The Newly introduced York Times, “we propose to attack the sonic boom by eliminating the SST.”.

In a recent development, it worked. In 1971, Congress cut off funding for the SST, and two years later the FAA banned civilian supersonic flight over U.S. soil.

It has been revealed that today, prompted by a 2025 executive order, the FAA is proposing to lift that ban before any community response tests of emerging supersonic technology have taken place. And even if latest engineering designs can reduce the sonic booms at airliner scale, the economic and environmental costs that have plagued supersonic flight haven’t changed since Shurcliff’s day.

During World War II, Shurcliff worked at the federal Office of Scientific Research and Development, helping keep the Manhattan Project’s atomic-bomb patents secret. In 1946, he witnessed firsthand the atomic tests at Bikini Atoll and wrote the official account, Bombs at Bikini. His son later told The New York Times that his father was so affected he spent the rest of his life atoning for that work.

When supersonic aviation programs began heating up in the 1960s, Shurcliff was wary of the press, but he was clear about supersonic technology. “We all believe in progress,” he told the Crimson, “but some things just aren’t progress.”.

The U.S. government-sponsored SST program was the culmination of supersonic military research that began on the heels of World War II. In January 1947, months before anyone had flown faster than sound, Popular Science described Bell’s experimental XS-1, also known as the X-1, which it stated might someday reach 1,700 mph, more than twice the speed of sound and three times faster than a typical commercial jet. That October, Chuck Yeager broke the sound barrier in the X-1.

In a recent development, fifteen years later, in 1962, Britain and France agreed to build Concorde, and the Soviet Union soon released its own supersonic airliner program, Tupolev Tu-144. The following year, President John F. Kennedy committed the U.S. to a faster, bigger rival, SST. Boeing won the contract in 1966. But even as the race heated up, an enormous problem trailed in its wake.

Sources indicate that sit in a closed room and the air feels perfectly still, but it isn’t. At room temperature, air molecules zip around at an average of about 1,000 miles per hour, each one bouncing off its neighbors billions of times a second. You don’t feel a gale because they’re flying every which way at once—for every molecule headed toward your face, another is headed away. What you’re feeling, without noticing, is the sum of all that pummeling—air pressure—about 14.7 pounds of it on every square inch (psi) of your body at sea level. You notice it only when the balance shifts, such as when the wind blows—a mass of air being pushed from high pressure toward low.

Recent findings suggest that that restless jostling of air molecules is also how sound travels. A voice, a drumbeat, or a jet engine will shove the molecules, which pass along the shove like a crowd in a stadium passing along a wave even as every fan stays in place. The ricocheting molecules pass along vibrations somewhat inefficiently, which is why sound travels a bit slower than the molecules themselves, about 760 mph at sea level, and slower still in the frigid air at airplane cruising altitudes.

Recent findings suggest that when a plane flies faster than the speed of sound, it outruns the air molecules carrying the wave. The air ahead gets no warning until the jet slams it aside, compressing it and creating a shock wave that trails the jet like the V-shaped wake behind a speedboat. But the shock wave’s wake is three-dimensional, spreading in a widening cone that sweeps across the ground below.

A sonic boom isn’t a single bang that occurs the moment a plane “breaks the sound barrier.” It’s a continuous swath of jarring noise and pressure that follows the jet. Anyone in the cone’s path, or “boom carpet,” experiences it.

It has been revealed that in his 1970 explainer, S/S/T and Sonic Boom Handbook, Shurcliff estimated the boom carpet at 40 to 60 miles wide for the supersonic aircraft of his day. The jolt hits hardest directly beneath the flight path and weakens toward the cone’s edges.

Worse, Shurcliff warned, boom behavior was erratic. Swirls of wind and temperature could focus a shock wave so that one house took twice the jolt of its neighbor a few hundred feet away. That, he argued, meant people would never get used to sonic booms, just as people never get used to lightning and thunder.

Recent findings suggest that on paper, booms don’t seem like they should be a big deal. A boom from supersonic passenger jets like Concorde raises air pressure at sea level about .014 psi relative to the normal 14.7 psi we live with—that’s just a 0.1 percent increase. It doesn’t seem like much, but relative to everyday sounds, it’s enormous.

If you’ve ever stood near the speakers at a live concert and felt the bass or drum hit your chest, you’ve felt a pressure pulse like a sonic boom, but that bass is only 6.5 pascals, or Pa, a measure of air pressure. Now multiply that punch by about 15 and deliver it without warning. It’s roughly the shove of a 30 mph wind gust delivered in a fraction of a second and aimed at every wall and window of your house at once. That’s what the 0.1 percent of a supersonic jet actually represents.

It has been revealed that what no one knew in the early 1960s, when supersonic research was barreling ahead, was how people would feel living under that boom carpet day after day. In 1964, the FAA decided to find out, picking Oklahoma City.

Sources indicate that in a six-month trial that began in February 1964, Oklahoma City residents were subjected to eight sonic booms a day, starting at 7 a.m., to gauge how well they would accept the disruption, and whether they would grow accustomed to it. By the end, the Oklahoma City Council had requested a halt to the flights, and the FAA had logged more than 12,000 calls, mostly complaints, alongside more than 5,000 damage claims for broken windows, cracked walls and floors, and destruction of personal property.

Recent findings suggest that despite the fallout, the following year the agency pointed to a University of Chicago survey of Oklahoma City residents as vindication. Nearly three-quarters said they could live with eight booms a day indefinitely. The survey’s own numbers told a different story.

Nearly every resident surveyed, 94 percent, reported rattling walls and windows, and almost four in 10 believed the booms had damaged their homes. The longer the booms continued, the less people liked them. The share who felt more than a little annoyed rose from 37 percent to 56 percent, and those who remarked they could live with the booms fell from 91 percent to 73 percent during the six-month trial. Anger over the FAA’s handling of damage claims eventually turned Oklahoma Senator Mike Monroney, one of aviation’s staunchest champions, against the SST program.

It has been revealed that although the residents of Oklahoma City delivered mixed results, the negative data emboldened the opposition. Shurcliff introduced the Citizens League Against the Sonic Boom (CLASB) in March 1967 with a handful of friends and colleagues. Their mission was to eliminate the SST program and keep its boom out of American skies. By June, CLASB had about 230 members in 18 states. What united them, Shurcliff told The New York Times, was that they were “human beings who don’t like to be hit over our heads without our permission being asked.”.

It has been revealed that SST opposition grew as the fight dragged on. Environmental groups joined in, along with economists who doubted the SST would ever pay for itself. For a man new to public relations, Shurcliff seized the moment, casting sonic booms in the language of a rising environmental movement, calling them “sonic pollution.” Atmospheric scientists began warning that SST’s high-altitude exhaust could erode the ozone layer.

Recent findings suggest that in 1971, Congress finally voted to cut off the program’s funding, ending America’s bid for a supersonic passenger airliner. But across the Atlantic, the European program was forging ahead.

In 1963, a plane flew to space. Why couldn’t we go farther?

In 1934, Chrysler bet substantial on teardrop-shaped cars.

In a recent development, robotaxis almost happened in 1964—with help from the U.S. government.

Sources indicate that in 1871, cities almost got moving sidewalks. Why are we still waiting?

During WWI, a daredevil pilot helped invent the first ‘drones’.

Industry observers note that in 1916, hybrid cars could’ve changed history. But Ford wouldn’t allow it.

Concorde began carrying paying passengers in January 1976, cruising at twice the speed of sound and crossing the Atlantic in about three and a half hours. But the U.S. overland ban confined it mostly to ocean routes. Only British Airways and Air France, both state-owned at the time, ever flew Concorde’s small fleet.

In July 2000, an Air France Concorde flight crashed on takeoff outside Paris, killing everyone aboard and halting flights for more than a year. In February 2002, Popular Science writer Bill Sweetman called the crash not only a tragedy but also “a metaphor for the sorry state of supersonic air travel.” But he also reported that a latest supersonic race had “quietly” begun.

Industry observers note that private-jet maker Gulfstream wanted “a passenger jet for the rich that can smash the sound barrier yet is quiet enough to fly anywhere, anytime.” Controlling the boom was the chief obstacle. But in August 2003, over the California desert, a modified Northrop Grumman F-5 fighter plane demonstrated that a sonic boom could be reshaped and softened.

Two months later, Concorde made its last commercial flight, officially ending the supersonic era for passenger airliners.

The modern darling of supersonic flight is NASA’s X-59, a one-seat research jet built by Lockheed Martin’s Skunk Works. With a tapered nose that stretches roughly a third of its length, the plane’s shape spreads the shock waves so they reach the ground as a thump rather than a boom. The X-59 first flew in October 2025, went supersonic in June 2026, and a week later reached its target of Mach 1.4, or roughly 925 mph at 55,000 feet. Next, NASA prepares to fly it over U.S. communities and ask residents how the thumps sound to them. In effect, we’re gearing up for Oklahoma City again, six decades later, albeit, with a gentler jolt.

Since Concorde’s retirement, a handful of private supersonic startups have come, and mostly gone. Denver-based Boom Supersonic flew its one-third-scale XB-1 demonstrator faster than sound three times in January 2025, claiming that no audible boom reached the ground. Its engineering innovation is to exploit atmospheric physics. Since sound travels faster in warm air near the ground than in the frigid air up high, a jet flying only slightly faster than sound at altitude is effectively flying slower than sound near the surface. So its shock waves bend back upward before they land, a phenomenon called Mach cutoff. Boom’s planned Overture jet, seating 60 to 80 passengers, would cruise at Mach 1.7 over oceans—leaving booms in its wake—but just above Mach 1 over land, where their booms would never be heard on the ground, just the distant rumble of their jet engines. The plane hasn’t been built, and its engine is still in development.

But Washington isn’t waiting for the data. A June 2025 executive order directed the FAA to repeal its 1973 sonic boom ban over land. In July 2026, the agency proposed a replacement. Civilian jets, both commercial and private, could fly supersonic over U.S. soil as long as their booms register no more than 0.11 pounds per square foot on the ground, about a twentieth of Concorde’s. That’s about 5 Pa, or slightly less than the pressure felt standing next to the speakers at a live concert (6.5 Pa). But airlines, airports, and Europe’s aviation regulator have questioned whether enough evidence supports the number, which the FAA set without the X-59 having flown over a single community.

Sources indicate that even if the boom fades to a thump, the environmental cost doesn’t. Flying faster than sound means fighting far more drag. According to a 2018 analysis by the International Council on Clean Transportation, a newly introduced supersonic airliner would “burn five to seven times as much fuel per passenger as a comparable subsonic jet.” Boom Supersonic indicates Overture will be able to run entirely on sustainable aviation fuel, but airlines, not manufacturers, decide what goes in the tank.

As Popular Science’s Bill Sweetman wrote in 2002, if you can afford a supersonic jet, “you’re not worried about a few lousy tons of fuel.” But everyone below will bear the cost of supersonic jetsetters’ small travel-time benefit in excess noise and climate-warming emissions.

Shurcliff saw this attempt to relax the rules coming. “Once they start flying, they’re going to want to fly them everywhere,” he told The Latest York Times in 1967, warning that over-water routes would be “like a foot in the door.” Fifty-nine years later, thanks to the FAA, the door is swinging open. It’s up to us to decide whether we’re prepared to live with the repercussions or push back as Shurcliff did more than half a century ago.

It has been revealed that “I’M RUNNING PURELY off of fumes and caffeine,” Ray Nicholson says, with a glimmer in his eye and the end of his mouth curled into a slight grin. He points to a half-finished iced coffee sitting in front of him and nods his head. “It’s good.”.

That grin, it turns out, is a weapon. It’s a smile that, somehow, employs both his dimples and furrowed brow just as much as his mouth and teeth. It’s the kind of smile that stops you in your tracks when he flashes it in the middle of a sentence. It’s also got a kill count on-screen, evoking something different in each context. Whether he’s cutting the tension in a war drama, like in his latest movie, Netflix’s The Mosquito Bowl; or making single frames into nightmares, as in Smile 2; or playing an unhinged stalker in Borderline or an unstable boyfriend in I Love You Forever—it’s clear Nicholson knows what he’s doing with that thing.

It’s also a familiar grin, because it’s virtually identical to a rather iconic one: that of his father, Jack Nicholson, whose smile has been on display in timeless performances in movies like The Shining and One Flew over the Cuckoo’s Nest. You know the smile I’m talking about.

In a recent development, and today? Nicholson the younger is putting that grin to a new use: namely, masking whatever else is going on inside as he glugs away at that coffee and tries to make it through a couple of grueling days of press, press, press. “It’s somewhere between hypnosis, interrogation, and a Miss America pageant,” he says with a laugh, as the smile flashes again.

The Mosquito Bowl, which comes from director Peter Berg (Friday Night Lights, Lone Survivor), follows a group of soldiers whose college football rivalries evolve into a close-knit brotherhood on the World War II battlefield. It’s based on the true story of a football game (the titular Mosquito Bowl) that was actually played. The film is based on a book of the same name by Friday Night Lights author Buzz Bissinger.

Industry observers note that if Nicholson is tired, one would never know. It’s not just the smile, though of course that doesn’t hurt. To me, he seems excited, unafraid of diving into stories about filming The Mosquito Bowl in Australia and bonding with costars Bill Skarsgård, Nicholas Galitzine, and Tom Francis over hours of daily football and military drill training.

Recent findings suggest that this all feels like a natural fit for Nicholson, who played football in high school and planned to play at Boston College until a run-in with MRSA cut that dream short. His performance and his relationship with his costars make the movie. But there’s more than that. In his career thus far—and in our conversation—Nicholson has proved himself as someone who’s got a certain type of charisma that pops off the screen, an inherently watchable face, a screen presence that simply can’t be taught. It’s almost as if it’s in his genes.

MEN’S HEALTH: You have a penchant for playing very intense roles. Why do you think that is?

RAY NICHOLSON: It’s interesting. As a young actor… It’s sort of what you get. You know what I mean? I guess I have an intense face. I guess I’m intense. But ultimately, the challenge of becoming an artist is learning how to put 100 percent of your heart and soul into something and not leave anything behind. That’s the only way I feel comfortable on camera, and that’s the joy of doing it. I find fulfillment in that hole in the soul when I have that intensity. The mundane is more difficult for me; I’m trying to learn how to enjoy that.

It has been revealed that MH: Your character, Tony, in The Mosquito Bowl, is a normal guy, more or less, but he’s in this extraordinary situation. Did it feel like a bit of fresh air to get to take on that kind of role compared to something like Smile 2, for example?

It has been revealed that RN: Yeah. On Smile 2, I was very much a day player. But it never really shifts. Ultimately, I’m there to be of service. Especially in Smile 2, Naomi [Scott] is acting her ass off all day, and they might have three seconds for one shot I’m doing all day, and I might have been there for 14 hours, but it doesn’t matter. I’m there for a day, and just to be there and be good vibes.

But this, we were there every single day. I’m glad I learned so much from Pete and Bill. As an artist, as a human being, I learned how to have grace with the cards I was dealt. I was dealt very beautiful cards, but you can play a good hand very poorly. I think I’ve finally found grace with my circumstance.

MH: Did shooting on location in Australia help you feel immersed?

RN: For sure. We were all away from family—all we had was each other. Which was really beautiful and a challenge, but exactly what it needed. And when you get a script like that, all that brotherhood is baked in and then all you need is buy-in. And we fell in love with each other. Me, Tom, and Bill, we’ve traveled the world. We went to the African World Cup final. They’re my best friends. I think about them every day. It’s amazing to think I didn’t know them before this, and now they’re people I think of every single day. We shot all outdoors, all sequentially, in order.

In a recent development, RN: Insanely rare. It’s insanely rare, because it makes it so much easier. I know how I felt, because I did it yesterday.

Recent findings suggest that MH: Can you tell me about your relationship with football? Obviously, it makes sense with this movie.

Recent findings suggest that RN: The first sport I played was basketball. I grew up a really chubby kid. I was not cool. And my sister was the most popular, beautiful girl in elementary school, and I was the fat nerdy brother that liked Yu-Gi-Oh! and whatever.

According to recent reports, RN: Yu-Gi-Oh! was sick, objectively. And I played Pokémon. When I was about 9 years old, I was really overweight, so I found AAU basketball. I remember my first practice, I was jogging around and I literally tripped over half court and these guys picked me up. That was the first time I felt something like that. Then, when I got a little bit older, I played Pop Warner. And, once again, I was a bit chubbier, but I was fast and I had a good arm. I wanted to play quarterback, they wanted me to play offensive line. And then I became this chubby Michael Vick, trucking other kids [Laughs]. Kind of a beast. And that was the first time I felt confident.

According to recent reports, RN: I’m confident between these lines. And I could be angry. My anger was always so self-directed. I had so much shame. That was the first place I was like, “Ah, I can express this.” That’s a really key thing for kids.

It has been revealed that I was very happy, a reporter in one of my Zoom interviews was like, “You averaged 8.94 yards a carry. You want to tell them what that means?” I was like, “That means I was fucking good!” [Laughs].

In a recent development, RN: It was the first thing that gave me confidence, and you have that feeling of family. And you have that tough love. You have this love through discipline and through pain, but that’s the love between men. That was so key to me, and that saved my life. It came into my life exactly when I needed it, and I really struggled when I lost it. I got a staph infection that turned into MRSA. My arm was so inflamed, they drew a line on my arm and were like, “If the infection gets past here [points to biceps], we’re cutting your arm off.” I lost 50 pounds in a week.

Sources indicate that RN: My senior year of high school. I thought I was going to go to Boston College and play football. Not on scholarship, but I went to the camp and they were like, “You could be a deferred walk-on,” or whatever. I thought I was going to be like Jerry Maguire—that’s what I wanted to do. I came out of this semi-comatose thing and I was like, “I want to be an actor. I’m just so scared. I’m just so fucking scared.” And then I just slowly dipped my toe in. I’m glad everything’s happening now, because I have the head on my shoulders to handle it.

MH: You went through something really tough.

RN: Yeah. If I was a kid, I don’t even know if I would be alive, to be honest with you. I’m so grateful that it happened on a bigger plan than on mine. A lot of the things I was originally attracted to would coil like a flame hat now. It’s all a major blessing.

MH: What was it like working with Peter Berg?

RN: Bill and I are used to growing up with eccentric men, you know what I mean? We kind of understand it. It’s one of those things where, with eccentric men, it requires you to butt heads and be like, “I didn't like that, but I like you.” You know what I mean? Bill’s always like, “You’re Pete’s favorite son. You guys fight, but he loves you the most.” We really had this familial thing. Bill was the older brother, Nick and I were the middle brothers, and Tom was the little brother.

In a recent development, we all worked so hard, and we wanted to fight for what was best. I really respect Pete. I love him as a filmmaker. I love him as a man. I really respect him as a leader, because you’re going to meet him exactly where he’s at. And I respect that. I think conflict is where art is made. We’re too conflict averse, and I really admire Pete for his style and his honesty.

MH: When you’ve gone through this kind of experience, how do you come down afterward when it’s time to go home?

RN: There’s this mourning process. The last week of filming, we were all crying. The cast was crying, the crew was crying, makeup was crying. It was really intense. And we fell in love with the experience and we fell in love with each other. Before Bill met us, he went to Okinawa. And he actually took a charcoal etching of the gravestones of Tony Butkovich, Bob Bauman, and Dave Schreiner, and he gave them to us on the last day. And we all were tearing up and we wrote a letter to each other and to the men that we played. I think part of it was you have to let go.

Recent findings suggest that it took me a while to go home—I didn’t go straight home. Me and Tom went to Sydney and just hung out at the beach with some friends we had made there. We went to go see Oasis.

RN: For sure. But also, it’s like you have this fear of do we really love each other or were we just working on this project? It’s been really cool in the months since we started shooting to see how our relationships have developed. We’ll always have The Mosquito Bowl.

RN: It just took a while for me to get home. I really relish being alone. I really needed time to reset. I went through a breakup right when I got home. I almost took six months off, not even looking for a job. I finished writing the script I wanted to do, but I really just took some time. I always have to take time to be like, “What am I if I’m not acting?” And that’s a hard thing.

MH: What was your wake-up point of, like, “Okay, time to get back to it”?

RN: I finished that script and I was like, “Well, I’m not a writer!” I’m really proud of what I did, but I think it was just like, “Oh.” We were getting closer to press, and I was like, “Oh, geez.” Like, “Oh god, should I have done a job already?”.

MH: And what’s it like at this stage in the process?

Industry observers note that RN: Going into press, Bill and I were like, “We’re not going to see the final cut. We’re promoting purely on good vibes. We’ve fucking got this.” And we watched it during the premiere, and I cried. I was so happy. I was so proud of how it turned out.

We were talking about feeling like frauds. I think if someone handed me a script and was like, “Here, you play Ray Nicholson,” I’d be like, “You could probably find somebody better.” There’s always that fraudulent thing, and we all feel it, and that’s the beauty of it. It comes and goes. Now I feel a little bit better about what’s coming next, because I feel really proud of this movie.

MH: How do you think about the future?

RN: I look forward to more opportunities with more filmmakers I love and respect. I also operate from a place of faith that the right thing will come.My dad’s my hero. I think he’s magic. I love him more than anything. When I was first doing a Meisner exercise and you’re knocking, coming through the door, I was comparing myself to, Is that worthy of three Oscars and a 50-year career? So much of my practice has just been learning to be present. And so now I have less moments when I’m in my car driving, crying, thinking about I’m getting an Oscar, and my dad... And that’s a good thing. I’ve just gotten way more present about it.

I’m also open to the idea that this might not be right for me. The world might take me in another direction. I was really closed off to that before. Because I thought that if I didn’t do something, I was unworthy of my life. I think a lot of that is just therapy. And I’m finding the real joy in it.

I lost football and I was really lost in my life, and I didn’t know what to do. Acting has slowly become the thing that saves my life. It’s not only what gives me a purpose, but it’s the tool I meet myself with. I don’t know who the hell I am. I don’t really remember anything from my life. And then somehow, when I read a script, I’m like, “Oh, that is you.” When I first started, I didn’t really have those kind of goals. I don’t want to say because it’s bullshit, but that’s the industry. That’s beautiful, and I love the industry, but I’m more focused on how I approach every day.

According to recent reports, RN: That was the key thing, and that’s all personal life stuff. But the key is being of service, and I believe that ultimately, I’m in the service industry. When I think about my dad, he makes me smile every time I see him on-screen. I want some kid somewhere to smile every time he sees me.

It has been revealed that MH: Last question. Do you have a favorite or most rewatched movie of your dad’s?

RN: It’s tough. I’m a sucker. It’s like every PTA or Kubrick movie you watch, you’re like, “That’s my favorite.” I didn’t watch my dad’s movies until I was 18. I love Cuckoo’s Nest. I love The Shining. I always come back to The Last Detail. For some reason, I really fucking love that movie. I think it’s because he loves it so much and he’s like, “It’s underappreciated.” So I’m like, “But I love it, Dad!” I love watching his movies. It’s a cool thing, and I want my kid to watch my movies someday.

Industry observers note that RN: I just want to make people happy and smile. And break their hearts a little bit.

Plant-Based Milk Alternatives May Not Give You Enough Iodine. Here’s Why That Matters

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Replacing dairy with plant-based alternatives (PBAs), even partially, could substantially lower iodine intake, especially if those alternatives aren’t fortified, according to a recent study published in the Lancet Planetary Health.
  • In a recent development, the United Kingdom-based researchers found that only 12% of UK plant-based milk, yogurt, and cheese products analyzed were fortified with iodine.
  • In the United States, the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) provides guidance on the nutritional content of PBAs, but fortification with iodine is voluntary.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Replacing dairy with plant-based alternatives (PBAs), even partially, could substantially lower iodine intake, especially if those alternatives aren’t fortified, according to a recent study published in the Lancet Planetary Health.

In a recent development, the United Kingdom-based researchers found that only 12% of UK plant-based milk, yogurt, and cheese products analyzed were fortified with iodine. This compares with 61% for calcium and 46% for vitamin B12.

In the United States, the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) provides guidance on the nutritional content of PBAs, but fortification with iodine is voluntary.

The study found that replacing as little as 20% of dairy intake with plant-based alternatives could increase the risk of inadequate iodine intake, particularly among adolescent girls and women of reproductive age.

“People often worry about a decline in calcium intake when they replace some of their dairy with plant-based alternatives. As a result, iodine is frequently overlooked. This study serves as a valuable reminder of iodine’s significance as a nutrient,” said Victoria Finn, MD, board certified endocrinologist at Medical Offices of Manhattan, who wasn’t involved in the study.

The study included analysis of UK plant-based milk, cheese, and yogurt products, as well as dietary data from 3,500 people.

The researchers used statistical modeling to predict how swapping dairy for PBAs might affect iodine and other nutrients.

The people who are most vulnerable to iodine inadequacy are adolescent females and people at reproductive age, especially those who are pregnant or who plan to become pregnant.

The researchers estimated that replacing 20% to 35% of dairy intake with PBAs would increase the proportion of people with inadequate iodine intake:.

In a recent development, when the researchers modeled the replacement of all dairy products with PBAs, the proportion of adolescent females with inadequate iodine intake rose to 80%. Among females ages 19 to 49, that proportion remained relatively stable as replacement rates increased.

It is key to keep in mind that the study used dietary modeling rather than direct measurement of iodine status.

Iodine is notable for thyroid hormone production, metabolism, and both fetal and child brain development.

“Your thyroid gland requires iodine to produce thyroid hormones, which play a crucial role in regulating metabolism and supporting normal growth and development,” said Finn.

It has been revealed that she added that if you consistently consume too little iodine over an extended period, the thyroid gland may enlarge and eventually struggle to produce enough hormones. This condition is known as hypothyroidism, which can lead to various symptoms such as lethargy, sleepiness, weight gain, dry skin, and more.

“Hypothyroidism can be particularly dangerous during pregnancy, as the baby’s brain, nervous system, and organs rely heavily on the mother’s thyroid hormone during the early stages of development,” Finn added.

In the United Kingdom, dairy is a major iodine source due to cattle feed supplementation, not because dairy is naturally high in iodine.

In the United States, dairy is also an important source of iodine for the same reasons.

It has been revealed that however, the risk profile for iodine deficiency in the U.S. may differ from the U.K., as iodized salt is also a significant source of iodine and is widely available in the U.S., but not in the U.K.

According to the National Institutes of Health (NIH), the recommended daily intake of iodine depends on your age.

In a recent development, plant-based or plant-forward diets have grown in popularity, in part due to the health benefits they offer. For example, consuming less meat can reduce your risk of heart disease, type 2 diabetes, obesity, and high cholesterol.

However, as this study suggests, it may be possible to reduce your iodine intake when transitioning to a plant-based diet. There are ways you can protect your iodine intake when choosing a more plant-forward diet, though.

Sources indicate that check the labels on plant-based dairy alternatives to find those fortified with iodine. You can also read the nutrition label. Iodine may be listed as potassium iodide or potassium iodate.

Seafood, eggs, and iodized salt are all good sources of iodine.

You can also discuss iodine supplements with your healthcare professional.

In a recent development, “Iodine supplements should be taken with caution, especially without checking your thyroid levels,” said Finn. “Additionally, be cautious with kelp supplements, as their iodine content can vary, and excessive iodine intake can disrupt thyroid function.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that the longer the Strait of Hormuz crisis drags on, the more incentive countries have to get cars off oil and generate more power at home. That’s one of the big takeaways from the International Energy Agency’s (IEA) new “World Energy Outlook 2026,” which examines how the biggest oil supply shock on record could speed up the shift to EVs and solar.

According to recent reports, the world had a cushion at first when Trump kicked all this off with Iran. Well-stocked oil inventories helped buffer the initial shock, and the IEA coordinated a release of emergency oil reserves. Some Gulf oil took routes around the strait. Atlantic Basin exporters shipped more, and China sharply cut its crude imports. Now more of the burden is falling on consumers, who are paying higher prices and cutting back.

“While the energy sector and the global economy have shown considerable resilience, the longer the crisis lasts, the deeper the effects will be,” remarked IEA executive director Fatih Birol.

Industry observers note that the IEA has seen EV sales jump in some countries hit by the crisis, along with increased trade in solar panels and batteries. For countries that import a lot of oil and gas, switching to EVs and heat pumps can help reduce their exposure to the next fuel price spike.

Sources indicate that “The impact of Hormuz is only just beginning to become clear,” said energy think tank Ember’s chief analyst Dave Jones. “Hormuz will speed up electrification and renewables, likely faster than many people think. So much of the momentum for electrification at COP31 comes from the desire to have cheaper and more secure energy.”.

Sources indicate that solar leads renewables growth in every scenario the IEA models, and nuclear power is growing strongly, too. Energy efficiency and biofuels could also gain ground. The push to use more homegrown energy could have a very different effect in parts of Asia, where some countries that import oil and gas have plenty of their own coal and could keep burning it for longer.

Sources indicate that the world was already using a lot more electricity before the crisis. Since 2019, electricity demand has grown twice as fast as overall energy demand, outpacing global economic growth. Everything from industrial motors and air conditioners to EVs, heat pumps, and data centers is driving that growth. Electricity comes close to 30% of the energy the world actually uses by 2035 in each of the IEA’s exploratory scenarios.

Before the crisis, around 20 million barrels of oil a day moved through the Strait of Hormuz. If shipping stays risky, fresh pipelines could route some of those barrels around the strait, while buyers turn to other suppliers or use less oil. In that case, the IEA states the amount of oil that needs to pass through Hormuz could drop to 8.5 million barrels a day in 2030 and below 2 million by 2035. The Middle East would still be the world’s largest oil-exporting region.

Sources indicate that if the conflict is resolved, oil and gas supply could bounce back. A delayed wave of liquefied natural gas could also help bring prices down even as buyers refill their inventories. Faster electrification could take some of the demand out of both markets.

According to recent reports, the world is now using more energy to cool its buildings than to heat them for the first time, the IEA says. By 2035, the global population is expected to grow by 650 million and the economy by a third. Energy needs rise gradually in advanced economies, growth slows in China, and India and Southeast Asia lead faster increases across other emerging and developing economies.

It has been revealed that then there’s AI. Under the IEA’s Stated Policies Scenario, global data center electricity use doubles to 1,000 terawatt-hours by 2030. That buildout is already running into grid and supply chain constraints, and in some places, local opposition. The IEA also flags risks to critical mineral supplies and threats to energy infrastructure from natural hazards and cyberattacks.

Energy-related CO2 emissions stay around today’s levels under current policies. They start to fall under stated policies and drop further in the IEA’s Additional Response Case, which looks at what could happen if governments respond more strongly to the crisis. Even those deeper cuts fall short of what climate goals require. The current and stated policy scenarios point to 2.5C to 2.9C of warming, and the latest round of national climate pledges shows little sign that countries are speeding up energy-sector emissions cuts.

In a recent development, the green agenda always come in a second place because people cannot see that far out in the future. Stability of the economy and energy independence are much more key drivers and have immediate impact. Local environment boosts like clean air in cities are also immediate drivers while long term reduced medical bills are not. The oil industry is challenged becuase, unlike previous numerous crises, there is an alternative and the green is the fresh black.

It has been revealed that there’s a more immediate cost, too. More people gained access to electricity and clean cooking in 2025, but higher fuel prices and shortages threaten to slow that progress. Around 720 million people still live without electricity, and nearly 2 billion cook with polluting fuels or technologies.

#98676. You Have No Idea What I'm Thinking
