  • In any case, the Saab car brand has been dead for precisely a decade, but now an auction is selling off a unique piece of automotive history that has deep ties to the now-defunct marque.
  • According to recent reports, the entire Emily GT project, which surfaced in 2023 after being developed in secrecy for half a decade, is being auctioned off in Sweden by Klaravik.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that I don’t really know why, but I’ve always been fascinated by Saab, the ill-fated Swedish car manufacturer. Maybe it’s because it was always a little left-field, even when it was part of General Motors, or maybe I liked the cars’ design.

In any case, the Saab car brand has been dead for precisely a decade, but now an auction is selling off a unique piece of automotive history that has deep ties to the now-defunct marque.

According to recent reports, the entire Emily GT project, which surfaced in 2023 after being developed in secrecy for half a decade, is being auctioned off in Sweden by Klaravik. The lot includes a working mule prototype, bodies, parts, accessories, drawings, and four complete Emily GT prototypes, which are billed as the only ones that will ever be available on the open market.

According to recent reports, developed by ex-Saab engineers who worked at NEVS, the company that picked up the pieces after the storied automaker’s bankruptcy in 2012, the Emily GT was envisioned as a next-generation electric model with four in-wheel motors and a driving range of up to 600 miles, courtesy of a high-voltage battery that could, in theory, top out at 175 kilowatt-hours. According to technical drawings obtained by SaabPlanet, the standard-range car would have had a 105-kWh pack, while the mid-spec model was designed for a 140-kWh pack.

Wireless charging at up to 11 kW was also in the cards, and no fewer than four body styles, including a shooting brake, a sporty sedan, a two-door coupe, and a cabriolet.

Sources indicate that the four electric motors, developing a combined 490 horsepower, enabled a quite sophisticated torque vectoring system, leading to great road manners. However, none of it materialized. NEVS never had the cash to move forward with the project, and now all of the pieces are being sold off.

“For us, this is a historic event, and I believe many Saab fans feel the same way,” said Nina Selander, CEO of NEVS. “Despite only ever being built as a handful of prototypes, the Emily GT has achieved iconic status. That says a lot about the fascination with the car. By making the sale available in this way, we hope to attract car enthusiasts all over the world whose hearts beat for Saab.”.

For the right buyer, it’s the perfect starter kit for a latest car tech giant, but it won’t come cheap. According to the Swedish local newspaper Ttela, the starting bid will be roughly $1.5 million (15 million SEK), and the auction house is not splitting the lot’s components into individual pieces. Everything is bundled into a single lot, so whoever has the highest bid goes home with everything.

Separately, Klaravik is auctioning off the world’s only NEVS Sango, a prototype of a self-driving vehicle designed for public transport that never materialized.

Both online auctions will go live on November 25 and will run through December 9.

#98549. Bears don’t sleep all winter, and other cold-weather animal myths

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (947 w)
📖 Baca
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Popsci ↗ Open Full Page

Bears don’t sleep all winter, and other cold-weather animal myths

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (947 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that it’s almost winter in the Northern Hemisphere.
  • That brings to mind a number of misconceptions people have about animals in the winter.
  • Recent findings suggest that many of us learned in school or on TV that bears sleep all winter.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that it’s almost winter in the Northern Hemisphere. While the humans fire up their furnaces (or, ideally, heat pumps), animals prepare in their own ways.

That brings to mind a number of misconceptions people have about animals in the winter. Most of us were taught things that, over time, were proven to be untrue, and winter behaviors are no exception. Bears, for example, don’t sleep the entire winter. Birds don’t actually care about the cold that much, and migrate for other reasons. And squirrels aren’t constantly forgetting the location of their nuts. Let’s dig into these common winter myths, and what actual research points to.

Recent findings suggest that many of us learned in school or on TV that bears sleep all winter. It’s not true—bears don’t hibernate. At least, not exactly.

An explainer published by the National Park Service states that hibernation isn’t a black-and-white concept: “In recent years the view that the state of hibernation exists on a spectrum rather than as a binary yes-or-no condition is becoming more entrenched.” The piece goes on to say that black bears don’t hibernate as deeply as smaller animals.

There’s real research backing this up. A 2011 study published in Science by researchers at the University of Alaska Fairbanks shows that bears get up and shift position throughout the winter. “Animals changed position twice a day to once every 2 days, when they stood, occasionally groomed, and rearranged bedding material,” the study states. The research also states that bears use a great deal more energy during the winter than smaller animals. “During torpor, metabolic rates of small hibernators decrease to 2 to 5 percent of basal metabolic rate (BMR),” the study explains, before showing that bears’ metabolic rates reach closer to 25 percent. That’s a wide spectrum.

So bears don’t sleep all winter—they regularly get up. That brings us to another myth: The idea that bears give birth without waking up. It’s also not true, according to the National Park Service.

“They’re not only awake during this time, but in the days before birthing, expectant mothers will often add bedding to the den by chewing materials into smaller pieces and arranging them just-so,” the explainer states. “After the 1 to 3 half-ounce to 1 lb cubs are born, she meticulously licks them clean, and provides warmth and mother’s milk as they grow to about 5 lbs by the time they emerge in spring.”.

Which isn’t to say that bears are active in winter—they really do slow down. But they don’t hibernate to the same extent as smaller animals.

Industry observers note that you might think that birds fly south for the winter because they don’t want to freeze—we even call cold-hating humans who travel in winter “snowbirds,” in reference to this belief. But it turns out birds aren’t directly concerned with cold weather.

Industry observers note that if you have a bird feeder you’ve probably noticed that many birds stick around for the winter.An explainer by the Cornell Lab of Ornithology states that birds are perfectly capable of surviving winter temperatures. “Escaping cold temperatures is not itself a major factor that drives birds to migrate, since many species, even hummingbirds, can withstand freezing temperatures as long as an adequate supply of food is available,” the article states.

There’s less food around in the winter, and that’s the actual reason for migration. You might say this is semantics, and you’re not entirely wrong—the cold temperature causes the food shortage. But if you’re picturing shivering birds, desperate to travel somewhere warmer, you’re imagining the wrong motivation. Birds don’t leave in pursuit of warmer weather; they leave in pursuit of food and longer daylight hours. And they head back north (or south) in the spring for the same reason: the thaw means a lot of fresh food, not to mention safe, open areas for breeding.

According to recent reports, squirrels spend a good part of the year hiding nuts, all so they can recover them in the winter. A common legend goes something like this: squirrels forget about most of these nuts, and that’s how forests grow. And while it is true that squirrel caches can become trees, squirrels don’t forget their nuts that often.

They are, in fact, really good at keeping track of their nuts, and this has been known for decades. A 1991 paper published in Animal Behaviour by researchers at Princeton University revealed this. In the study, captive grey squirrels were all given hazelnuts to bury in the same area. The nuts were then all removed by experimenters. The squirrels were re-introduced to the site, one by one, with a twist: experimenters buried fresh nuts in the squirrel’s own 10 cache sites and an equal number of sites randomly chosen from caches made by other squirrels.

The results were striking. “Although each squirrel’s own caches were close to the caches of other squirrels, the squirrels retrieved significantly more nuts from their own sites than from sites used by other squirrels, after all delays,” the paper states. “The retrieval accuracy of the squirrels under these conditions indicates that while grey squirrels can locate buried nuts by their odour, they can also remember the individual locations of nuts they have buried.”.

Other studies show how well squirrels can remember nuts. A 2023 study published in Urban Ecosystems by researchers from Poland found that hazelnuts cached by squirrels are more likely to be dug up than hazelnuts buried by humans in the same area. This suggests that squirrels are pretty good at remembering where they buried their nuts.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Are you a port or rail terminal operator looking for a latest electric material handler that can move serious cargo without sacrificing maneuverability? Do you wish it had tank treads? If that’s you, the Mantsinen 200 might be just the thing.

Designed to handle demanding port and rail terminal operations, the Finnish-built Matsinen 200 material handler combines impressive reach and lifting capacity with the ability to move around a worksite on its own tracks. And, yes: I said tracks.

In a recent development, by far the most fun feature of the Mantsinen 200 is the fact that it looks like a rejected concept for a ROBOTIX dinosaur set and/or something He-Man would use to run over Trap Jaw. And while, yes – most substantial material handlers have similar form factors, there’s something about the 200 that really sells the whole Dragon Walker vibe.

It has been revealed that the Mantsinen 200 is powered by a 380 kW (~510 hp) grid-connected electric motor running at 1,800 rpm. Power comes from a 460V electrical connection as standard, with other voltage options available to suit local site requirements.

Recent findings suggest that mantsinen says its electrically powered machines deliver the same performance as their diesel counterparts, while eliminating exhaust emissions at the machine and reducing operating noise, energy consumption and maintenance costs. Power is delivered through a load-sensing hydraulic system featuring four variable-displacement piston pumps and a separate closed-loop swing circuit.

Industry observers note that mantsinen also fits the 200 with its proprietary HybriLift energy-recovery system. HybriLift works a lot like regenerative braking by capturing potential energy as the main boom is lowered, but instead of storing that energy as electricity in a battery, the material handler stores it in hydraulic accumulators for reuse during the next lift. The organization claims HybriLift improves the massive machine’s energy efficiency by up to 50%, effectively giving the machine an additional 300 (ish) hp of lifting assistance at average lifting speed.

In a recent development, and, while the machine normally draws power from the grid, operators aren’t necessarily tethered to an outlet. Mantsinen offers an optional PowerPack that allows the machine to disconnect from its main power supply and still travel around the worksite, with some basic hydraulic systems still functional. The PowerPack is presently diesel-powered, but a battery-backed version isn’t out of the question. It’s a useful bit of flexibility for terminal operators who want the benefits of electric material handling without giving up the ability to reposition the machine when a fixed electrical connection isn’t available.

Industry News: Two-Thirds of Dementia Content On TikTok Is Misleading, Researchers Say

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1014 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Healthline

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A latest survey suggests that about two-thirds of dementia advice videos on TikTok are misleading.
  • Of the videos examined, the analysis indicates that nearly half contained inaccurate and potentially damaging information.
  • The researchers say that approximately 44% of TikTok creators who share dementia content lack credibility and appropriate qualifications.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A latest survey suggests that about two-thirds of dementia advice videos on TikTok are misleading.

Of the videos examined, the analysis indicates that nearly half contained inaccurate and potentially damaging information.

The researchers say that approximately 44% of TikTok creators who share dementia content lack credibility and appropriate qualifications.

Although misleading dementia content may appear on other social media platforms, this research examined only TikTok content, warranting further investigation.

The survey was commissioned by Homewatch Caregivers and has not been published in a peer-reviewed scientific journal.

Recent findings suggest that A spokesperson for TikTok told Healthline that if health-related content is potentially harmful, it is flagged for removal. The spokesperson added that 99.6% of misinformation deemed violative was proactively removed from the platform in 2026.

Sources indicate that the spokesperson added that TikTok relies on fact-checking and guidance from public health authorities to help assess the accuracy of content. The platform may also apply warning labels to content that cannot be verified as accurate.

Sources indicate that looking to social media for health information is not uncommon. A recent poll reports that 31% of adults in the United States use social media at least once a month to look for health information and advice.

Experts advise seeking information about dementia from trusted sources, such as a primary care doctor and organizations like the National Institute on Aging (NIA) and the Alzheimer’s Association, rather than social media, where content creators who share advice often lack expertise.

“It’s normal to want answers quickly when you’re caring for someone living with dementia, and a short video from someone who seems to know what they’re talking about can be really convincing,” mentioned lead researcher Jennifer Winarski, senior manager of care operations and quality for Homewatch CareGivers.

It has been revealed that “Despite there being some genuinely helpful information out there, you don’t always know whether it’s backed by medical evidence, so we wanted to bring our own expertise to uncover whether popular TikToks can be trusted,” she told Healthline. “We hope our report will encourage people to be a bit more careful about what they act on.”.

For the survey, researchers selected a sample of 500 of the most-watched dementia-related videos on TikTok with hashtags such as:.

Researchers then transcribed the video data to assess its accuracy.

The researchers found that two-thirds (66.4%) of the popular TikTok videos contained misleading information. Of those videos, about half (47.6%) contained potentially damaging misleading dementia information.

“It’s clear that many of the creators mean well, but much of what we saw was personal opinion rather than proven information, and in a few cases, general good health tips were presented as if they were specifically helpful for individuals living with dementia,” Winarski said.

“If families act on that, they could end up spending time and money on things that won’t help — and in the worst of cases, it could delay getting the support their loved one really needs,” she added.

Dung Trinh, MD, an internist for MemorialCare Medical Group and chief medical officer of the Healthy Brain Clinic in Irvine, CA, stated it’s vital to be aware of the volume of misleading dementia information on social media. Trinh was not involved in this survey.

Some people may be making decisions about their health based on incomplete, misleading, or incorrect information, he mentioned.

“For example, someone might see a video claiming that a particular supplement can reverse Alzheimer’s disease or that certain memory problems automatically mean someone has dementia,” Trinh stated.

“These messages can lead to unnecessary fear, false reassurance, wasted money, or delays in getting a proper diagnosis.”.

“We are entering an exciting era in Alzheimer’s care, with advances in blood-based biomarkers, earlier detection, and treatments that may slow disease progression in appropriately selected patients,” Trinh continued.

“Getting an accurate diagnosis and receiving timely medical guidance are becoming increasingly important.”.

The researchers examined the content creators behind the TikTok videos included in their analysis. They found that 44% of video creators behind the misleading videos had no relevant qualifications.

Rehan Aziz, MD, vice chair of education in the Department of Psychiatry at Hackensack Meridian Jersey Shore University Medical Center and associate professor of psychiatry and neurology at the Hackensack Meridian School of Medicine in Upcoming Jersey, said that content creators offering dementia advice should have relevant qualifications. Aziz wasn’t involved in the survey.

“Start by looking at the creator’s profile for a full name and a specific credential, such as MD, DO, PhD, or RN, along with a specialty,” Aziz told Healthline.

“For dementia, the most relevant experts include neurologists, geriatric psychiatrists, geriatricians, neuropsychologists, and nurses, including advanced practice nurses, or social workers who specialize in dementia care.”.

“You can confirm a doctor’s license through your state’s licensing board website and check board certification at certificationmatters.org,” Aziz said.

As of 2020, more than 55 million people worldwide were living with dementia — a neurological condition that negatively affects the brain. Researchers predict this number will hit 78 million by 2030.

The increase in the number of people seeking dementia content online is a reflection of this trend.

When looking for accurate dementia information and guidance, Nestor Beltre, MD, a neurologist with Baptist Health Kenneth C. Griffin Neuroscience Institute, part of Baptist Health South Florida, stated a great first step is to speak with their primary care physician. Beltre wasn’t involved in the survey.

“Memory changes can occur for many different reasons, and some causes, including vitamin deficiencies, depression, and certain medical conditions, may be treatable,” he told Healthline.

“Early evaluation can help identify what may be contributing to these changes and determine the most appropriate next steps. Depending on the individual’s symptoms, a neurologist, psychiatrist, or neuropsychologist can provide further evaluation and guidance,” Belter continued.

Beltre advised turning to trusted resources such as the Alzheimer’s Association and the National Institute on Aging, which can increase public understanding of memory-related conditions and available treatment options.

“The most vital message is that patients and families have resources available to help them better understand and manage cognitive health,” he noted.

Industry observers note that so, you think you can run an electric car firm? Well, here’s your chance to prove it. An entire electric vehicle development project is heading to auction this month, and it comes with almost everything you need to get started. There's even a connection to one of the automotive industry's most beloved defunct brands: Saab.

Sources indicate that as first brought to our attention by Great Britain’s Car, Swedish auction manufacturer Klaravik is preparing to sell the entire NEVS Emily GT project. The auction includes four complete prototype vehicles, a fifth development mule, spare body panels, parts, tools, and engineering drawings. And unlike a typical automotive auction, where you might leave with a single vehicle, the winning bidder gets the entire collection.

A little backstory is helpful here. After Saab Automobile closed its doors in 2012 following an ill-fated tie-up with Spyker, a Chinese consortium called National Electric Vehicle Sweden (NEVS) acquired the majority of the remaining assets, including the Trollhättan factory, manufacturing equipment and intellectual property. However, NEVS was not interested in building a next-generation Saab 9-3 Aero. Instead, they had their sights set on building an electric car future.

Their vision of that was called the Emily GT, envisioned as a sophisticated electric grand touring sedan capable of competing with established luxury EVs. Development began in late 2019, and just 10 months later, the Emily GT rolled out into view. And much like Saabs of the past, the Emily GT had some unique features—the most obvious being its four electric motors, one mounted inside each wheel. Combined, they produced a healthy 490 horsepower.

Industry observers note that however, while the power output was healthy, the financial condition of the company was not. NEVS never secured the funding necessary to bring the car into production. The ambitious project remained stuck in the prototype stage, where it’s stayed frozen .

According to recent reports, so, do you think you’re the right person to bring it to market? If so—or even if you’d rather just own a very odd automotive dead-end—Klaravik will open online bidding on November 25, with the auction scheduled to conclude December 9. All four completed vehicles and the accompanying development materials are being offered together rather than individually.

Industry observers note that of course, buying the prototypes and engineering materials doesn't automatically give someone a functioning car manufacturer or guarantee a path to production. Manufacturing, regulatory approvals, and financing would still present enormous challenges. However, if you do happen to be an ambitious entrepreneur with deep pockets, this could be your chance to revive an electric vehicle that never had the chance to see the light of day.

#98545. Breaking: Mysterious volcanic rock discovered in the Mariana Trench

Breaking: Mysterious volcanic rock discovered in the Mariana Trench

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (826 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that space exploration tends to suck up most of the oxygen when it comes to venturing out into the unknown.
  • Recent findings suggest that that absurd depth and bone-crushing pressure make Challenger Deep brutally difficult to study.
  • Using the remotely operated Jason/Medea submarine robot, the team documented evidence of pyroclastic rocks (the shattered debris of violent eruptions) on the trench wall some 20,000 feet below the surface.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that space exploration tends to suck up most of the oxygen when it comes to venturing out into the unknown. But there’s an arguably even more mysterious frontier hidden beneath us. Nowhere is that more real than at Challenger Deep. The deepest known point on Earth, Challenger Deep is located in the 1,580-mile-long Mariana Trench at the floor of the Pacific Ocean. Getting to the bottom of this ancient chasm means diving more than 6.8 miles (around 36,000 feet) underwater. For a sense of scale, Mount Everest could be dropped into this chasm, and its summit still wouldn’t reach the surface.

Recent findings suggest that that absurd depth and bone-crushing pressure make Challenger Deep brutally difficult to study. As a result, assumptions about what lies down there rarely hold up for long. Scientists long believed the area’s frigid, pitch-dark depths couldn’t sustain life, until a pair of divers reported animals near the seafloor in 1960. Now, a team using a robotic submersible in the trench says they have found the deepest evidence of explosive volcanic eruptions ever documented in the ocean.

Using the remotely operated Jason/Medea submarine robot, the team documented evidence of pyroclastic rocks (the shattered debris of violent eruptions) on the trench wall some 20,000 feet below the surface. Finding those kinds of rocks there was unexpected and will change the way geologists view the area. Writing today in the journal Frontiers in Earth Science, the researchers say their discoveries may also “help explain why the Challenger Deep is so deep.”.

“Explosive volcanism near trenches is unusual, so we were very surprised,” Dr. Robert J. Stern, a geologist at the University of Texas at Dallas and study co-author, remarked in a statement. “These are the deepest pyroclastic rocks documented to date from anywhere in the ocean.”.

Reaching the depth needed to study the Mariana Trench takes some serious equipment and preparation. In 2012, Titanic director James Cameron famously made the dive with a specially designed submersible that reportedly cost around $10 million to build. In this case, the team of scientists turned to a veteran robotic system called Jason/Medea. Part of the National Deep Submergence Facility and funded by the National Science Foundation, Jason/Medea traces its earliest version back to 1988. From the outside, the ROV somewhat resembles a Zamboni machine used to surface ice skating rinks.

Recent findings suggest that the robot can operate as deep as 21,385 feet below the surface, thanks to a roughly six-mile long fiber-optic cable connecting it to a vessel on the surface. Jason is equipped with a video and still-imaging systems. Its footage travels up through Medea, a companion robot that  hangs slightly higher in the water to buffer Jason from the motion of the vessel above. In addition to taking photos and videos, Jason has mechanical arms he can use to collect rock and sediment samples. The robotic duo has completed hundreds of dives around the world, analyzing hydrothermal vents in the Atlantic and Pacific Ocean, and even visiting a 1,600-year-old sunken Roman trading ship.

Industry observers note that in this case, the scientists deployed their robot companion in late 2024 along a 341 mile segment of the trench near Challenger Deep. Over seven dives, the robot team covered around 186 miles, taking photos and videos along the way. Analyzing the footage, the human team determined that the eastern part of the stretch is deeper than the western part and has steeper trench walls. They came across the old volcanic rocks on that steeper western side, seen below arranged in a thin flat layer. Exactly where these rocks erupted from remains unclear.

In a recent development, ”We haven’t identified the eruption sites yet,” Stern added. “We know that these hot pyroclastic flows moved down slopes, but we don’t think they moved very far. They retained enough heat to re-weld themselves into pretty hard rocks, and that heat would’ve been lost if the pyroclastic flows traveled great distances.”.

According to recent reports, the unexpected rocks were only one part of the expedition. The team also set out to study fragments of older, exposed crust and mantle. They also tasked the robot with studying the Shinaki Seep Field, one of deepest known hydrothermal vents sites on the planet. There was some cleanup duty as well:  the team recovered fluid-sampling devices left behind by a previous group of Japanese scientists in 2016. Explorers have rather glibly documented human trash all the way down at the bottom of Challenger Deep but these scientists, at least, won’t be adding to the litter.

If it does pass muster for on-road use where you live, these trucks are surprisingly plucky to drive, and would make for the ultimate DIY partner. The bed is also surprisingly flexible, with fold-down sides that transform it into a mini-flatbed truck. The payload is stouter than you'd think, rated for 770 pounds, so though it may be tiny, it's still mighty.

The selling dealer has recently replaced the battery and done a mild tune-up, including new spark plugs and an oil change.

#98543. Toyota just built a tiny folding electric bike to fit in your trunk

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (854 w)

Toyota just built a tiny folding electric bike to fit in your trunk

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (854 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Toyota is getting into electric bikes.
  • The Japanese automotive giant has unveiled the BKE Concept, a tiny folding electric two-wheeler designed to serve as a compact companion vehicle for short trips, outdoor adventures, and last-mile transportation.
  • Industry observers note that and when Toyota states compact, it means it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Toyota is getting into electric bikes. Well, sort of.

The Japanese automotive giant has unveiled the BKE Concept, a tiny folding electric two-wheeler designed to serve as a compact companion vehicle for short trips, outdoor adventures, and last-mile transportation.

Industry observers note that and when Toyota states compact, it means it. The little electric ride can reportedly fold up in around 30 seconds and become small enough to fit inside the trunk of the brand’s GR86 sports car. Think of it like Toyota’s take on the Motocompacto.

The BKE Concept was unveiled as part of the newly revived Scion by Toyota brand, which the manufacturer is positioning less as the return of the quirky youth-oriented car brand many Americans remember and more as a sort of experimental mobility laboratory.

In a recent development, toyota calls the upcoming Scion a “freedom lab” where the company can explore vehicles and mobility concepts that don’t necessarily fit neatly into its conventional automotive lineup. Alongside the BKE, Toyota showed its KEI-01 ultra-compact utility truck and a hybrid side-by-side.

But perhaps unsurprisingly for me, it’s the tiny electric two-wheeler that caught my attention.

In a recent development, and I should point out here that while Toyota refers to it as an “electric bike” in its own brand literature, the lack of pedals means that the cute little two-wheeler is not going to qualify as an electric bicycle in Europe or North America. The moniker means it merely slots into the broader electric bike category that encompasses everything from electric bicycles to scooters and motorcycles. In essence, the BKE is more or less a small seated e-scooter, sometimes referred to as a “no-ped”.

Despite looking like the kind of concept vehicle that might have been whipped up for an auto show, Toyota notes the BKE has actually been under development for several years.

A small team of chassis and electrical engineers has reportedly been testing and refining the design based on real-world use and feedback.

The basic idea came from a fairly simple question: How could Toyota make short-distance mobility easier and integrate it more seamlessly into everyday life?

The result is essentially a secondary vehicle designed to travel inside your primary vehicle.

According to recent reports, toyota specifically highlights camping, errands, last-mile transportation, and even using the BKE as a pit bike alongside a GR86. The bike can also be recharged from the 110V AC outlets found in many Toyota vehicles, meaning the car carrying it can effectively serve as its mobile charging station.

Believe it or not, Toyota Chairman Akio Toyoda has apparently been involved in the testing process himself. Toyoda attracted attention after riding a similar small electric mobility device around the 2025 Japan Mobility Show, and Toyota notes his experience riding prototypes has even resulted in design changes.

After Toyoda complained about getting splashed while riding through puddles, for example, engineers enlarged the rear fender.

It’s a small detail, but it’s also a pretty textbook example of Toyota’s famous kaizen philosophy of continuous improvement.

Here’s where things get a little frustrating for those of us who want to know what the BKE can actually do.

Sources indicate that toyota hasn’t unveiled the motor power, battery capacity, range, top speed, or even the vehicle’s weight. There’s also no pricing because, for now, there’s nothing to buy.

Toyota is referring to the BKE strictly as a concept and hasn’t unveiled production plans or a timetable for bringing it to market.

But the fact that Toyota indicates a small engineering team has spent several years developing and testing the BKE makes it more interesting than your typical one-off styling exercise.

And the underlying idea makes a lot of sense.

In a recent development, I’m obviously a massive believer in matching the vehicle to the trip. Taking a 4,000-pound car several miles to move one person isn’t always the most efficient solution, and a compact electric two-wheeler gives drivers an easy way to leave the larger vehicle behind for those shorter trips.

Toyota itself makes essentially the same argument, saying that using smaller vehicles for shorter journeys could reduce emissions by better matching the vehicle to the task.

There’s also something amusingly circular about one of the world’s largest automakers arriving at the conclusion that sometimes the best vehicle for a trip is a tiny electric bike.

In a recent development, but hey, I’ll take it. Now Toyota just needs to actually build the thing – and preferably tell us how fast it goes first.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that hyundai absolutely knocked the teasers for then Hyundai N Vision 74 out of the park. I mean, a hydrogen-electric hybrid that's an actual sports car, with all the style of a 1970s wedge car? The internet loved the idea. But, unfortunately, that's probably what the N Vision will remain—an idea. The prepares for production are on ice.

Recent findings suggest that simon Loasby, the head of Hyundai's Design Center, explained toThe Drive that the decision came down to business. When the South Korean automaker simply couldn't justify the business case for the car, it decided to not move forward with production in the foreseeable future. Here's what Loasby told the publication when asked if the automaker planned to make a production version of the N Vision 74:.

It has been revealed that at the moment, no. We were really on it. We had the production clay model of it and the exterior, interior, and so on.

It has been revealed that it comes down to the maths of how you judge what the business case is. And that if you’re very tight with the business case on only that car, the volumes of that car and the impact, you got no chance.

If you open it to the overall brand-raising profile value of that, you have a bigger chance. But as yet, [no].

Many of you reading this are likely part car lover and part EV enthusiast. Me too, which is why I'm immensely disappointed that Hyundai decided to cancel aims to build this awesome concept.

Industry observers note that after all, EVs are damn fun. Instant torque, low center of gravity. It's pretty much everything that an an enthusiast wants out of a sports car—even if EVs inherently are a bit heavier and lack a row-your-own gearbox. It also used the beloved Stinger as a base to build the car. But rather than the 3.3-liter twin-turbocharged V6, Hyundai stuffed it with the Nexo's hydrogen fuel cells and two electric motors.

That said, not all has gone to waste.

One of the coolest parts of the coupe was its retro styling. That was inspired by the original Hyundai Pony coupe, which was designed by the legendary Giorgetto Giugiaro (the same guy who designed the VW Golf, DeLorean DMC-12, and a plethora of other icons).

Loasby indicates that Hyundai's head of design, SangYup Lee, convinced the company not to throw away the design work from the N Vision concept. Instead, it reused some of the design elements for new models like the all new 2027 Hyundai Elantra.

"[T]hat top view as you notice, even in the pillar and side view up to the roof crease and the flatness of the roof, that’s all playbook N74," he told The Drive. He later hinted more could be coming: “Just imagine what an N version of [Elantra] can be. It’s really good, it’s awesome.”.

Recent findings suggest that maybe it was the idea of using hydrogen that killed the N Vision concept. Or perhaps that coupes have seem to go the way of the dodo in recent years. Whatever the reason, it's just unfortunate for enthusiasts who were pumped to see a sport-tuned FCEV in the distance.

According to recent reports, one glimmer of hope is that Loasby didn't say that the car is dead forever. Just that Hyundai couldn't make a business case for it "at the moment." Perhaps we might get something with two-doors, a striking design, and battery power in the future. Until then, I'm staying pumped about the Rivian R3X.

Fancy axes and simple pottery show how interconnected Europe was 5,000 years ago

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (537 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Today, the Rhine River stands as a physical border between parts of France and Germany, and a cultural boundary between Western and Central Europe.
  • It has been revealed that sebastian Schultrich, an archaeologist at Kiel University in Germany, looked at late Neolithic coarse pottery, double axes, and collective graves from either side of the Rhine and found significant cross-boundary ties in the late 4th and early 3rd millennia BCE.
  • “The combination of pottery, burial rituals and tools reveals fresh insights into life 5,000 years ago,” Schultrich said in a statement.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Today, the Rhine River stands as a physical border between parts of France and Germany, and a cultural boundary between Western and Central Europe. This physical and cultural separation seems to have existed for a very long time. Archaeological evidence on either side of the river as early as the late fourth millennia BCE reveals differences. Archaeologists have determined that the river is a sort of barrier during this time—but new research challenges this conclusion.

It has been revealed that sebastian Schultrich, an archaeologist at Kiel University in Germany, looked at late Neolithic coarse pottery, double axes, and collective graves from either side of the Rhine and found significant cross-boundary ties in the late 4th and early 3rd millennia BCE. His findings, described in a study recently published in the archaeological journal Germania, suggest that populations in Western, Central, and Northern Europe were more connected than previously assumed.

“The combination of pottery, burial rituals and tools reveals fresh insights into life 5,000 years ago,” Schultrich said in a statement.

Industry observers note that the pottery in question, called coarse ware, is simple and plain—so much so that archaeologists have seen it as culturally insignificant. The roughly-shaped artifacts have emerged in many regions of Europe. It became widespread in modern-day central and northern France as well as the western Alpine region starting in the mid-4th millennium BCE. Afterward, it also became prominent in modern-day western and northern Germany and Denmark.

“There are indications that a convergence of pottery styles across such great distances occurred gradually and unconsciously. This is an indicator of high mobility within a region where there were no distinct barriers between groups, or where the boundaries were fluid,” remarked Schultrich.

It has been revealed that double stone axes—prestigious axes with two cutting edges and a shaft hole—were also widespread in this period. Archaeologists have discovered them from France through Central Europe to Scandinavia and Poland. While the dates of the French double stone axes has been a subject of contention, it’s right now clear that they, along with the Central and Northern European versions, hail from the the 4th and early 3rd millennia BCE. Unlike coarse ware, the double axe design seems to have been intentionally widespread, showing that a shared concept existed on either side of the river.

The same regions are also home to different versions of large-scale group burials, including passage graves or gallery graves. But they all were the final resting place of dozens to hundreds of individuals, were used over many generations, and were the locations of ritual acts and gatherings. This is more evidence of a shared idea, even though its regional manifestation differed.

Recent findings suggest that “It was not a uniform cultural complex,” Schultrich explained. “What we see here is a network characterised by fundamental narratives, yet one that simultaneously allowed scope for strong regional peculiarities. This is an early example of a complex, differentiated form of society in which identity combined both supra-regional and local elements.”.

By drawing prehistoric connections across the Rhine, Schultrich revealed ties across late Neolithic Europe that clearly overcame the watery boundary.

Tesla Cybertruck’s already impressive turning radius gets even tighter

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tesla is rolling out an update that makes the Cybertruck turn even tighter, improving on what was already one of the best turning radiuses you can get in a full-size pickup.
  • Recent findings suggest that but there’s a catch.
  • In a recent development, tesla’s official Cybertruck account posted a short drone video early Saturday showing a truck doing circles in a parking lot, with a “before” and “after” comparison of its turning path.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tesla is rolling out an update that makes the Cybertruck turn even tighter, improving on what was already one of the best turning radiuses you can get in a full-size pickup.

Recent findings suggest that but there’s a catch. It only works on 2027 model year Cybertrucks, and Tesla intends to stop building the truck by the end of next summer.

In a recent development, tesla’s official Cybertruck account posted a short drone video early Saturday showing a truck doing circles in a parking lot, with a “before” and “after” comparison of its turning path. “Even tighter turns now rolling out to upcoming Cybertrucks,” the account wrote.

In a follow-up post, Tesla noted the improvement requires software version 2026.44 or newer and “only applies to model year 2027 Cybertrucks.”.

It's not the size … it's how you maneuver itEven tighter turns now rolling out to new Cybertrucks pic.twitter.com/FuNoox4ax0.

Tesla didn’t share a new turning circle figure. In the video, the “after” circle is visibly smaller than the “before” one by what looks to be at least a foot.

The Cybertruck’s maneuverability comes from its rear-wheel steering paired with steer-by-wire. At low speeds, the rear wheels turn opposite to the fronts, which shrinks the space the truck needs to make a U-turn. We’ve been tracking the Cybertruck’s four-wheel steering since the prototype days, when Tesla was showing it off in parking garages.

It has been revealed that even before this enhancement, the results were impressive. Tesla’s owner’s manual lists the Cybertruck’s curb-to-curb turning circle at about 43.5 ft (13.25 m). That beats the Ford F-150 Lightning at roughly 47.8 ft and the Rivian R1T at 44.9 ft, and it’s within about 4 ft of a Model Y. Not bad for a 6,600-lb truck that’s nearly 19 feet long.

It has been revealed that and Tesla always said there was more to come. At launch, the rear wheels turned only about 3 degrees. In early 2024, a Tesla engineer said a software enhancement would push that to 10 degrees, and Elon Musk said the manufacturer had improvements in the works to “tighten the turning circle significantly.”.

Tesla hasn’t said whether this revision delivers the full 10 degrees, or why it’s limited to 2027 trucks. If it comes down to hardware, owners of earlier Cybertrucks who were counting on this as an over-the-air upgrade are out of luck.

Industry observers note that credit where it’s due. The turning circle is one of the best things about the Cybertruck, and anyone who has driven one knows it. Steer-by-wire combined with rear-wheel steering is real engineering, and other vehicles are just starting to get that combo a couple years after Cybertruck had it. Making it even better is a nice update.

But it’s hard to get excited about it.

And 39.4 feet turning circle for the Cadillac Escalade which also has rear wheel steering. As does the iX5 (39.7'), MB GLC (36.7') and EQS (35.8'), the Lucid Gravity (38.4), Hummer 37.4', Cayenne (38.4) and a around two dozen other vehicles on the market today. So maybe this is not such significant news after all?

It has been revealed that earlier this month, Musk announced that Tesla will wind down Cybertruck production at Gigafactory Texas to make room for Cybercab. He has since pushed the end date to the end of summer 2027 to work through an “order backlog.” We estimate Tesla is delivering about 7,000 to 8,000 Cybertrucks a quarter, roughly 12% of the 250,000 units a year it planned for.

So Tesla is improving a 2027 model year truck that it will stop making next summer. And since Tesla now only sells the $109,990 Cyberbeast, the people getting this upgrade are the few still buying the most expensive Cybertruck in its final months. It does nothing about what actually sank the truck: pricing that never came close to the $39,900 promised in 2019, range and towing that fell short, and a design most truck buyers never warmed up to.

It’s a cool engineering flex on a product with an expiration date. If Tesla had delivered this kind of polish on the $40,000 truck it promised, would we be writing the Cybertruck’s obituary right now?

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Volkswagen GTI badge has been a staple in automotive culture for 50 years, and it’s clearly not getting sidelined anytime soon. VW just released the ID.Polo GTI Clubsport concept, an electric track-focused GTI that slots in as the automaker’s fourth fresh GTI variant this year.

While it’s not heading to production, the Clubsport concept is a peek into the possibilities riding on the electric ID.Polo GTI, which became the first EV to wear the GTI badge when it was released earlier this year. The standard ID.Polo GTI, which isn’t sold in the United States, reaches 62 mph in 6.8 seconds thanks to a 223-hp electric motor mounted to the front axle.

See all results for Volkswagen ID.GTI for sale near 92604.

In a recent development, the Clubsport concept ups the ante, with VW claiming it will hit 62 mph in just 4.7 seconds with the help of launch control and a more powerful APP550 electric motor. The upgraded motor, which is typically used to power the rear wheels of larger models like the ID.Tiguan and ID.7, sends 362 horsepower to the front wheels and nearly doubles the standard electric GTI’s torque output from 213 to 406 pound-feet.

Industry observers note that volkswagen also equipped the concept vehicle with an electronically regulated front differential lock, a performance-tuned adaptive suspension system, and ceramic brakes with a one-box brake setup. The high-performance powertrain fits into an equally aggressive two-door build, complete with a large front splitter, diffuser, and a flared rear wing.

According to recent reports, rather than the typical five-seater setup, the Clubsport concept houses two Recaro bucket seats with red five-point harnesses. A Tornado Red roll bar replaces the rear seats, and the cockpit is solely reserved for racing needs, meaning the standard infotainment system is also omitted. The cabin is finished in a dark microfiber material and trimmed with red stitching.

Volkswagen calls this concept the “perfect match of heritage and future,” and the automaker says its young employees were involved in much of the concept’s realization. The ID.Polo GTI Clubsport concept won’t ever make it to VW showrooms, but it’ll be displayed next week at the Essen Motor Show in Essen, Germany.

Industry observers note that alayna Wilkening grew up reading motorsport magazines and following her grandpa around his Chevrolet dealership's showroom floor. In true Hoosier fashion, her first car was a hot pink custom cardboard "Fiero-vette" for her kindergarten Kindy 500 race. She now autocrosses a 1994 Miata with her dad, which she learned to drive the night before her first event. Alayna went to Indiana University and graduated with a degree in journalism and a minor in graphic design. As a testament to her great taste in cars, her first real one was a metallic orange 2007 Chevy HHR, which she lovingly called "The Dumptruck.".

💡 Key Takeaways

  • According to recent reports, earlier this month, insurer Allstate published the results from its 2026 Thanksgiving Driver Report.
  • It has been revealed that the data also demonstrated a similar, though not quite as extreme, pattern on Black Friday, presumably from people unaware there are Black Friday deals online.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, thanksgiving is, as Dominic Toretto might put it, all about family—which means it makes for one of the biggest travel weeks of the year in the United States. Typically, that means egregious traffic and delays on the Wednesday before and the Sunday after, whether you’re making your way by plane, train, or automobile. But apparently, Thanksgiving is also a time when many drivers satiate their need for speed.

According to recent reports, earlier this month, insurer Allstate published the results from its 2026 Thanksgiving Driver Report. The insurance company examined data on 44 million trips during Thanksgiving week in 2025, compared with a typical week in November. One major difference was drivers’ willingness to hit the gas pedal on Thursday morning: Allstate found that between 6 a.m. and 9 a.m. on Thanksgiving, the rate of drivers exceeding 80 miles per hour increased to 200 percent above the normal baseline—a tripling of the average—and it stayed at 100 percent above the norm through noon. South Carolina, Latest York, Texas, North Carolina, and Florida showed the biggest increases in speeding above 80 mph. (Allstate did not break down the percentage of those drivers who were stressed-out dads deliberately choosing to drive early Thanksgiving morning to make good time and receive commendations from others for having the foresight to travel at that less-convenient time.).

It has been revealed that the data also demonstrated a similar, though not quite as extreme, pattern on Black Friday, presumably from people unaware there are Black Friday deals online. Allstate found an 80-percent increase above normal for drivers exceeding 80 mph between 6 a.m. and 9 a.m.

Speedy driving, naturally, creates potential safety risks. Allstate estimates that about one-fifth of the drivers exceeding 80 mph were concurrently engaging in at least one other “risky behavior.” About 90 percent of those drivers engaging in risky behavior were using their phones. However, there were some who had better cause to than others; Monday after Thanksgiving produced the highest increase in roadside service calls for the week, running 52 percent above normal.

As one would expect, drivers are also traveling longer distances over Thanksgiving weekend. Per Allstate, the share of trips longer than 100 miles doubles on Wednesday and Thursday, and the average trip on Thanksgiving Day is 40 percent longer than usual. Which also, perhaps, could explain the desire to go fast.

GLP-1s Like Ozempic May Boost Brain Health, But Can They Lower Dementia Risk?

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (983 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Healthline

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, GLP-1 medications have transformed obesity and type 2 diabetes treatment.
  • A comprehensive newly introduced review published on November 5 in the journal Science evaluated the current evidence on how GLP-1 medications like semaglutide and tirzepatide may affect the brain across aging, cardiometabolic disease, and Alzheimer’s disease.
  • Industry observers note that the authors of the review suggested that GLP-1 medications like Ozempic and Zepbound may offer brain health benefits.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, GLP-1 medications have transformed obesity and type 2 diabetes treatment. Now, researchers are investigating whether the effects of this blockbuster class of drugs extend beyond weight loss and affect brain health.

A comprehensive newly introduced review published on November 5 in the journal Science evaluated the current evidence on how GLP-1 medications like semaglutide and tirzepatide may affect the brain across aging, cardiometabolic disease, and Alzheimer’s disease.

Industry observers note that the authors of the review suggested that GLP-1 medications like Ozempic and Zepbound may offer brain health benefits. However, they were also left with the question of whether the medications act directly on the brain or whether better brain health is actually a consequence of improved cardiometabolic health.

Sheena Aurora, MD, vice president, Medical Affairs, Alzheimer’s Association, who wasn’t involved in the review, told Healthline that more research is needed to better understand the effects of GLP-1 drugs on the brain.

“While research suggests GLP-1s could reduce brain inflammation, improve blood vessel health, and even protect neurons, much broader, randomized clinical trials on GLP-1s and brain health, including in people with Alzheimer’s disease and other dementias, are needed,” she said.

It has been revealed that GLP-1 medications like semaglutide, the active ingredient in Ozempic and Wegovy, mimic the GLP-1 hormone. Tirzepatide, the active ingredient in Mounjaro and Zepbound, also targets a second hormone pathway called GIP.

These medications have been shown to produce significant weight loss and improvements in cardiometabolic health.

Sources indicate that this is important for brain health because obesity, type 2 diabetes, and vascular dysfunction are all linked with cognitive impairment and dementia. Insulin resistance and chronic inflammation may also link metabolic and brain health.

According to recent reports, analyses of large outcome trials and observational cohorts have suggested that GLP-1 medications may be associated with a reduced risk of cognitive impairment and dementia. However, randomized trials in diseases like Alzheimer’s disease have yet to demonstrate clinical benefits.

Around 200 preclinical and mechanistic studies have shown benefits for learning, memory, synaptic plasticity, and neuronal resilience, though results are heterogeneous in design and direction, so a clear consensus on magnitude and mechanism remains lacking.

Industry observers note that it is also unclear how well GLP-1 medications reach the brain. They appear to reach certain areas, such as the hypothalamus, brainstem, and circumventricular organs, more readily than regions protected by the blood-brain barrier.

It has been revealed that the report authors noted that some studies have shown that GLP-1 receptor agonists may reduce the risk of cognitive impairment and dementia in people with type 2 diabetes. This may be due to cognitive challenges being linked to factors such as blood sugar, blood pressure, vascular health, and sleep.

Mir Ali, MD, medical director of MemorialCare Surgical Weight Loss Center at Orange Coast Medical Center in Fountain Valley, CA, who wasn’t involved in the report, told Healthline, “These findings are interesting, but like many of the other benefits associated with GLP-1 medications, a direct causal relationship has not yet been proven.”.

“Rather, the benefits appear to be more closely tied to the reduction in obesity and better control of diabetes,” he said.

Aurora noted that growing evidence supports the heart-brain connection.

She cited newly introduced findings from the Alzheimer’s Association’s landmark U.S. POINTER study presented at the Clinical Trials in Alzheimer’s Disease (CTAD) conference November 16–19 in Boston, MA.

The research demonstrated that the structured lifestyle intervention program also improved heart health risk factors, such as:.

“U.S. POINTER can change those risk factors within 24 months, and better heart health risk-factor control was linked with better cognition,” Aurora mentioned. “We’re also interested to see whether adding a drug like a GLP-1 to a U.S. POINTER-style lifestyle program improves cognition in at-risk older adults more than the program alone.”.

To find out, the Alzheimer’s Association is funding the Prevention of Risk for Cognitive Decline through Combined Therapy (PROTECT-Cog) global phase 3 clinical trial.

PROTECT-Cog is a first-of-its-kind trial designed to evaluate whether combining a proven multidomain lifestyle intervention with a metabolism-targeting drug, like a GLP-1, can further reduce the risk of cognitive decline, mild cognitive impairment, and dementia in at-risk older adults.

Dung Trinh, MD, internist at MemorialCare Medical Group and Chief Medical Officer of Healthy Brain Clinic in Irvine, CA, who also wasn’t involved in the review, told Healthline, “I often remind my patients that what’s good for the heart is generally good for the brain.”.

“The brain depends on a healthy cardiovascular system to deliver a constant supply of oxygen, glucose, and other nutrients. Conditions such as high blood pressure, diabetes, obesity, and high cholesterol can damage blood vessels, promote chronic inflammation, and increase the risk of stroke and vascular cognitive impairment,” he remarked.

“Over time, these changes can also contribute to the development or progression of dementia.”.

Trinh added that while GLP-1 medications can improve several cardiometabolic risk factors, these improvements do not automatically translate into proven dementia prevention.

“Regular physical activity, a heart-healthy diet, adequate sleep, and management of cardiovascular risk factors remain essential strategies for maintaining brain health as we age,” he mentioned.

When the report authors turned their attention to more stringent tests on semaglutide in people already living with early Alzheimer’s disease, the picture began to change.

Novo Nordisk’s EVOKE and EVOKE + Phase 3 Trials examined the efficacy of semaglutide in people with early stage Alzheimer’s disease.

The studies revealed that while semaglutide produced changes in several disease-related biomarkers, it didn’t slow the progression of Alzheimer’s disease.

This emphasizes that fixing metabolic concerns might prevent cognitive decline in someone with obesity or diabetes. But it might not be enough to reverse the damage in someone with established Alzheimer’s disease, where profound synaptic loss and protein pathology have already occurred.

The review authors suggest that future research on obesity and diabetes should also include rigorous and specific cognitive testing.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, A bird couple with a long history has laid their first (and likely only) egg of the 2026-2027 season. United States Fish and Wildlife Service (FWS) volunteer and photographer Dan Rapp spotted the egg on George and Geraldine’s nest this weekend. The pair are endangered short-tailed albatrosses (Phoebastria albatrus) or makalena in Hawaiian, and this is their 10th straight year together.

According to Friends of Midway Atoll, the pair did not produce an egg last year, making this arrival “especially exciting news.”.

Recent findings suggest that short-tailed albatrosses are almost completely white and have a large pink bill. The monogamous birds can live up to 50 years, and nest on islands and atolls where they typically lay one egg per season. Short-tailed albatrosses are listed as endangered, and biologists estimate that there are only 10,000 left in the wild.

George and Geraldine were banded as chicks on Torishima Island, Japan. They raised their first chick together during the 2018–2019 breeding season. The duo is the only breeding pair of short-tailed albatross on the Midway Atoll, but other members of their species were observed last season. After spending the summer/non-nesting season apart, George was first spotted at Midway Atoll on October 18. He was reunited with Geraldine by October 22.

This remote group of islands sit about 1,250 miles from Hawaii’s capital Honolulu and are most famous for a pivotal World War II battle. Every fall, it becomes a temporary home to the world’s largest albatross colony. Albatrosses are a group of large migratory seabird species. Some notable albatross species are the wandering albatross (Diomedea exulans), which has the largest wingspan of any living bird species and the Laysan albatross (Phoebastria immutabilis). At over 70 years old, a Laysan albatross named Wisdom claims the title of oldest known banded wild bird. She has produced roughly 50 to 60 eggs, and as many as 30 of her chicks have fledged in her lifetime, and she became a grandmother once again in March. Wisdom has not been spotted yet this nesting season.

Bird enthusiasts from around the world can eavesdrop on this albatross colony via live cameras and follow Friends of Midway Atoll National Wildlife Refuge for updates. Viewers can expect to see the birds return to the islands, perform courtship dances, begin to nest, lay their eggs, and eventually watch fluffy albatross chicks.

#98534. Void/Breaker Review – Chaos Is The Point

Void/Breaker Review – Chaos Is The Point

📅 03 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1016 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gameinformer

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Many games tout impressive destruction systems under the hood, but few implement it as well as Void/Breaker.
  • Industry observers note that void/Breaker wastes no time getting a gun in your hand.
  • This narrative framework supports the game’s roguelite structure.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Many games tout impressive destruction systems under the hood, but few implement it as well as Void/Breaker. The ruin is visually spectacular, sure – who doesn’t love to watch buildings crumble because of your grenade or gravity-thrown explosives? But importantly, it’s a critical aspect of Void/Breaker’s roguelite design. Enemies caught beneath falling rubble become instantly staggered, and that’s your moment to kill. Grenades do this too, as do most items you throw at the hostile AI machinery trying to end your run, creating a vortex of shifting priorities as you dash, jump, and shoot at sequential staggered enemies in your sightlines. Countless weapon mods and permutations make fewer than a dozen weapons feel like hundreds in your arsenal, adding even more blissful chaos to the mix. Though it can be difficult at times, if you can see through the literal remains of your destruction, one of the year’s most engaging shooters awaits.

Industry observers note that void/Breaker wastes no time getting a gun in your hand. An AI voice in your head wants your help escaping a simulation where thousands of runners attempt to reach the end of multi-arena stages to defeat a boss. He asks that you simply follow the simulation’s commands; meanwhile, he uses the data you collect along the way to find new exits for you and him. The storytelling style is very reminiscent of Valve’s Portal. Something much larger is at play here, but it’s worth discovering for yourself.

This narrative framework supports the game’s roguelite structure. Mechanically, however, you enter various themed digital stages, from liminal spaces to beaches to snow-capped cliffs and more, and attempt to survive. Most arenas consist of a couple of starkly white structures that your grenades and thrown explosives can topple (ideally onto waves of enemies below). Learning the language of Void/Breaker means constantly scanning your field of view for explosives and structures practically begging to come down, and then eyeing neon-green bars above enemies that tell you they’re staggered and ready for a quick kill. Developer Stubby Games throws plenty of wrenches into this formula, like armored foes and electrostatic enemies you must melee first, and elite bots that will have you on the back foot, but for the most part, Void/Breaker’s formula is “Break stuff, then kill.”.

The game emphasizes explosives and bringing buildings down, but your guns do most of the killing; you can only select one weapon per run. You choose from a pistol, shotgun, machine gun, sniper, and more, and each has its perks (though once I unlocked the SMG, I rarely picked anything else). There’s no sense overthinking your weapon, though, because the dozens of mods you pick up each run determine its effectiveness. As you pick up more schematics, the pool of mods you find in chests or drop from enemies expands, and soon your gun fires corrosive acid, electricity, fire, projectile missiles, and more. Not to mention, mods change how the gun fires, how much damage certain bullets do, recoil, accuracy, and just about any other stat you associate with firing a video game gun. Wild combinations are easy to create, and a unique mod-stacking mechanic that can double or triple effectiveness adds a light touch of puzzle design to this otherwise straight shooter.

It has been revealed that stubby Games smartly emphasizes player expression, never getting in the way of the zanier combinations available to players. The SMG I used to beat the final boss featured mods that made each bullet electric, shot missiles with each shot, covered each bullet in a destructive orb, and featured a ricochet perk that made each bullet bounce off walls and split into even more bullets. I’m thankful for mid-run saves because this SMG permutation, paired with an ability mod that let me throw infinite grenades for a limited time, filled my screen with so much destruction that the entire game crashed. I’d usually bemoan such a thing, but I couldn’t help but laugh. I pushed my PC to its limit with my on-screen chaos.

Sources indicate that boss fights leave a little to be desired – I rarely died because of their simple bullet-hell arenas. Instead, most runs ended because, after bringing down every structure around me, I’d get so lost in the chaos that I wouldn't realize I was stuck in debris while enemies swarmed my location. As stunning as it is to see so much happening on screen, it can be hard to understand what is going on during the most chaotic moments.

It has been revealed that between enemy-filled arenas en route to a stage’s end boss, you might find a shop to buy more mods, ominous obelisks with risk-reward propositions (gain a lot of health or lose half your health, for example), optional trials, and strange phenomena that transport you to different locations. These moments are quick breaks in between bouts of adrenaline-fueled shooter action that I always welcomed – enemies can be relentless, especially as new types are introduced in each stage.

Industry observers note that the rest of the Void/Breaker package offers few genre surprises. You can upgrade various traits between runs, research fresh mod schematics to add to the random pool, purchase new weapons, and discover fun secrets. You can unlock shortcuts, glean in-world information from computer terminals, and hear intriguing dialogue barks from the AI partner who needs your help. It’s all standard stuff for the rogue genre, but if anything, its simplicity pushes you back to the meat and potatoes of this shooter.

Recent findings suggest that void/Breaker’s shorter runtime – I rolled credits at 12 hours – ensures nothing gets too repetitive in its roguelite structure, but an expansive endgame promises even more to engage with, like different run modifications you can enable to make an already chaotic shooter even more anarchic. I’ll certainly be running it back (again and again) to see what other disruptions I can bring to this AI-simulated adventure. It’s hard not to when destruction feels this good.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I have to admit that when I first saw the Fangchengbao Tai 9 stow its steering wheel away on social media, I assumed that it was AI. It wasn't. This BYD brand's new SUV can indeed retract its steering wheel right into the dashboard. However, it’s not quite used for the reason you’d think.

The Tai 9 is a six-seat, plug-in hybrid SUV about the same size as the Cadillac Escalade IQ, and it sits at the top of the Fangchengbao range. BYD’s Chinese-market brand and naming structure can be confusing, but in essence, Fangchengbao is one of BYD's premium brands.

Power comes from two electric motors that produce 536 horsepower at peak, while a 1.5-liter turbocharged engine is responsible for any combustion-powered driving. The Tai 9 has a 66.5 kWh battery that is capable of BYD’s flash charging technology. The brand claims it can sprint from 10% to 97% in nine minutes.

Recent findings suggest that those are all very compelling specs, but the most interesting part of the Tai 9 is the top-of-the-line Foldable Smart Cabin trim. Since the Tai 9 uses a steer-by-wire system, the steering wheel can fold up and stow itself in the dashboard. BYD notes that takes about 10 seconds.

However, this isn’t for any sort of autonomous driving. China’s autonomous driving rules are strict, and no automaker in the country has approval for commercially sold eyes-off, hands-off driver assist features. Instead, the folding steering wheel is primarily for comfort and space, specifically when the car is stationary. Photos of the feature in action show that stowing away the steering wheel makes extra room for a little table setup.

This isn’t entirely unprecedented. The new trend in China is for large SUVs to be third spaces where buyers can comfortably hang out, even when they aren't driving. The Tai 9’s Nappa leather, comfy seats, and second-row folding screen are meant to make it a calming, relaxing space to spend time. It's similar in concept to what we’ve seen on the Zeekr Mix and SkyNomad N90 Studio.

Still, despite the Tai 9’s folding steering wheel not being for self-driving, I wouldn’t be surprised if it does show up in cars for that reason someday, as manufacturers strive to make cars that can truly drive themselves.

In a recent development, A car with no steering wheel at all might feel risky and uncomfortable to some car buyers, especially if it's like Tesla’s Cybercab, which can’t be driven manually at all above low speeds. Yet, if there were a backup to take control, I could see that putting some minds at ease.

The Fangchengbao Tai 9 is on sale in China for about $42,000. The top-of-the-line model with the foldable steering wheel is about $49,500.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that one of the most common questions asked by first-time EV buyers is about the cost of electricity. Whether they plan to charge at home or find charging in the wild, everyone wants to know what to expect when it comes time to top off their batteries. One EV owner did the math after two months of EV ownership and came up with a surprising number: $7 a month.

Whether we’re talking gasoline, diesel, or electricity, one driver’s fuel costs can look dramatically different from another’s. How far they drive, how often, and under what conditions can matter just as much as what they drive. And while EVs may offer the greatest benefits to rural drivers covering long distances, a Redditor going by Suitable-Truth-350 took a different approach, moving into a highly walkable city for the express purpose of driving as little as possible.

In a recent development, “My wife and I recently retired and moved from a car dependent, rural/suburban area to a large, walkable city with good light rail. Our goal was to drive as little as possible,” write Suitable-Truth-350. “We took delivery of an Ioniq5 in August. We still have a daily walking life, but we use the car to see friends in the country, shop or travel around the greater Chicagoland area. After 2 months, we finally charged it.”.

According to recent reports, the result? Suitable states it took less than 30 minutes to juice their Ioniq 5 back up to an 80% SOC, at a total cost of $13.

Sources indicate that “Driving the car is a pleasure,” they continue. “The pickup and smooth operation so different from our last ICE vehicle. First impression, we love the car and could never imagine going back to (a gasoline-powered car).”.

I’ve been saying it for years: drive an EV for a week and whatever range anxiety you might experience will disappear. And, while it seems like Suitable-Truth-350 didn’t have much range anxiety to begin with, it’s worth noting here that their situation isn’t that rare.

In their most recent national survey, AAA found that the average US driver covered less than 29 miles per day, with the vast majority weekly commuting totals falling well within the range of even the most affordable used EVs.

The same survey found that just 30% of Americans reported taking at least one road trip the previous summer, with an average one-way trip length of ~235 miles.

It has been revealed that that 235 mile trip might be too much for a car like the Fiat 500e, but even that car – the latest EV with the shortest EPA-estimated range you can buy in the US – can make a 235 mile trip with a single 30-minute stop to charge. And in 2026 and 2027, they’re sure to find plenty of places to charge, thanks to a public charging network that’s newer, faster, and far more built out than they probably think, with more fast-charging locations opening every week and modern charging speeds that make longer stops the exception instead of the norm.

Our two EVs raised our monthly electric bill by ~ $60/mo. and that's without solar. That wouldn't have paid for one gas fill-up for a week in our previous gas cars. I don't think this is even a question. If you can charge at home, it's cheaper. If you rely on public charging all the time then it's a mixed bag but still generally cheaper in most parts of the country. All said, we have three EVs now and my monthly electric bill for our entire house with six people is less than what we paid for fuel in one gas car.

In other words: your charging costs are probably going to be higher than Suitable-Truth-350’s seven-ish dollars per month, but with $4/gallon premium and $6/gallon diesel still very much the norm in 2026, it’ll probably be less than you think, too.

Ferrari 296 Challenge Stradale Is the Purest Prancing Horse in Years
